title: Molecular mechanism of menthol-induced TRPV5 channel inhibition

paper_content.abstract:
TRPV5 channels play a critical role in calcium homeostasis and are implicated in various pathophysiological
conditions. Here, we demonstrate that the monoterpene menthol, commonly used for pain and inflammation
management, is an inhibitor of TRPV5. Electrophysiology experiments reveal that menthol blocks ion
conduction through a slow blocker mechanism. Using single-particle cryo-EM, we determine the structure of
menthol-bound TRPV5, which shows menthol interacting with W583, a residue previously implicated in
channel permeation, gating and binding of endogenous modulators. These findings expand the repertoire of
TRPV5 modulators and suggest that menthol could serve as a scaffold for developing channel-targeting
modulators.
paper_content.introduction:
TRP channels are important regulators of cation transport in a myriad of organisms and tissues. Vanilloid
TRP channels consist of subtypes TRPV1-6 and constitute one of the most diverse subfamilies, including
members activated by temperature, lipids, and natural compounds that participate in various important
physiological and pathophysiological processes. Most TRPV channels exert their actions through calcium
(Ca2+) signaling or the regulation of Ca2+ homeostasis1.
Among the TRPV channels, TRPV5 has one of the highest permeabilities for Ca2+ ions over monovalent
cations, with a relative Ca2+ to Na+ permeability ~1002, a property it shares with its homolog protein, TRPV6,
with 70% amino acid sequence homology between both proteins 3,4. These channels are mainly found in
Ca2+-absorbing epithelia, such as kidney and intestinal tissues, where their main function is the reabsorption
of Ca2+. TRPV5 is primarily expressed in kidney epithelial cells, specifically localized to the apical
membrane of cells of the distal convoluted tubules (DCT) and connecting tubules (CNT) of the kidney,
where it functions as a highly selective epithelial calcium channel, playing a crucial role in Ca2+ reabsorption.
While TRPV5 is predominantly found in the kidney, it is also expressed at lower levels in other tissues such
as brain and bone, where it has been shown to be essential for bone resorption by osteoclasts5,6.
TRPV5 channels, similarly to most members of the TRPV subfamily, form a functional tetramer at the cell
surface assembled by subunits containing six transmembrane domains with large intracellular N- and C-
termini. The pore domain consists of the S5, loop, and S6 segments of each subunit, which assemble
symmetrically in a four-fold structure to create a central ion conduction pathway7,8. The re-entrant pore loop
of each subunit forms the extracellular part of the pore and functions as a selectivity filter, determining ion
permeability, with a single aspartic residue at position 542 acting as a Ca2+ selectivity filter9,10. The S6
helices line the intracellular pore and form the gate at its narrowest part. TRPV5 inactivates in response to
Ca2+ entry, a process mediated by calmodulin (CaM) binding to the channel11 promoted by the interaction
between the last residue at the end of the S6 gate of the channel, the highly conserved W583, with a C-
terminal lysine of the CaM, which blocks the flow of ions through the pore7,12. The disruption of CaM binding
leads to increased TRPV5 expression at the plasma membrane by avoiding channel retention in the
endoplasmic reticulum13. The tryptophan residue W583 is highly conserved in TRPV5 across various
species, but it is absent in other members of the TRPV family and is crucial for channel gating14.
TRPV5 channels display marked inward rectification and are constitutively open at negative potentials,
allowing for passive entry of cations into cells at the resting membrane potential. Regulation of TRPV5 is
mainly carried out by the control of phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PI(4,5)P2) lipid concentration,
which binds between the N-linker, S4-S5 linker , and the S6 helix to keep the channel open12. Signaling by
vitamin D, which mostly regulates expression of protein at the plasma membrane15 and by parathyroid
hormone, which acts through PKA phosphorylation16, also regulate the channel. The long-chain lipid acyl-
coenzyme A (LC-CoA) is a highly efficient activator of TRPV5 that binds to the same site as the endogenous
ligand PI(4,5)P2 and induces very similar conformation changes to open the channel17.
TRPV5 channels have a relatively limited pharmacology, with only a few known additional endogenous
activators, such as PKC activator 1-oleoyl-acetyl-sn-glycerol (OAG) and the b-glucuronidase, Klotho, that
hydrolyzes extracellular sugar residues of TRPV518,19. Conversely, TRPV5 is inhibited by synthetic
compounds, including TH-117720, cannabinoids21, and a higher specificity inhibitor, ZINC1798899022.
Econazole and miconazole are antifungal agents that act as inhibitors of TRPV5. These compounds bind to
a specific pocket situated between the S4 and S5 transmembrane domains23, which is shared with TRPV6
channels24 and likely act as allosteric inhibitors of channel opening. Additionally, ruthenium red is a non-
selective inhibitor of many ion channels. In the case of TRPV5, it binds to the pore domain, likely blocking
conduction and stabilizing the channel in a closed state24,25.
Menthol is a highly-membrane permeable monoterpene alcohol derived from the mint plant (Mentha sp.)
and a known activator of cold-sensing TRPM8 channels26. Menthol is an interesting compound that has
been associated with renal toxicity and impaired intestinal mobility27,28, which could be mediated in part by
TRPV5 and TRPV6 ion channels. Menthol also activates or inhibits other TRP channels, such as TRPV3,
TRPV1 and TRPA1, although the structural mechanisms involved are not known29–32. TRPV5 and TRPV6
are only 30 % similar to other TRPVs which suggests that different mechanisms of modulation by menthol.
Given its potential effects on renal and gut physiology, and lack of mechanistic information, we explored
menthol’s actions on TRPV5 channels. Here we show that it acts as a blocker of TRPV5. We show that
menthol inhibits current through TRPV5 expressed in HEK293 cells by producing long-lived closures, likely
corresponding to slow blocking events. We solve the structure of rabbit TRPV5 in complex with menthol by
cryo-EM and find that a key determinant of menthol inhibition is a tryptophane residue at position 583
located at the intracellular entrance of the pore. Mutations W583Q and I575S readily reduce the effects of
menthol, suggesting that they are important mediators of the menthol interaction. Our results expand the
repertoire of inhibitors of TRPV5 channels and have implications to understand possible effects of menthol
in renal physiology.
paper_content.results:
Menthol inhibits TRPV5 via a slow blocker mechanism.
First, we assessed the effect of menthol on the rabbit TRPV5 (rbTRPV5) by applying 500 μM menthol to the
external face of the membrane in outside-out patch configuration. Menthol rapidly inhibited more than 50%
of the current at all voltages without altering current kinetics (Figure 1a). This inhibitory effect was largely
reversible and occurred in a dose-dependent manner across all tested voltages (Figure 1b, c, d). Fitting the
dose-response curve with a Hill equation (Equation (1)), we determined a half-maximal inhibitory
concentration (IC ) of 142.6 μM and a Hill coefficient (n ) of 0.75, suggesting that a single menthol
50 H
molecule is sufficient to induce inhibition (Figure 1e).
Interestingly, menthol block of TRPV5 is slightly voltage dependent, with the blocked fraction reduced at
less negative potentials (Figure 1f). Because menthol does not carry a net charge, we sought to explain this
voltage-dependence by exploring the predictions of a multiple state model for block. We adapted a
previously published three state gating model of TRPV5 14 and incorporated open state block (Scheme I,
Figure 1g). To constrain the model, we measured the voltage-dependence of single-channel channel
openings, which indeed show that TRPV5 gating is intrinsically voltage dependent (Supplementary figure 1a
and c). Scheme I explains the voltage dependence of menthol block because it is coupled to the open state
and opening is itself voltage-dependent (Figure 1g). This model also accounts for both the voltage and
dose-dependence of block with the same set of parameters (Figure 1e).
Since the sequence of the inner pore region is highly conserved between mammalian TRPV5 and 6
channels, we examined the effect of menthol on the human TRPV5 orthologue and the related human
TRPV6 channel, finding that both channels were also blocked by menthol with similar efficacy
(Supplementary figure 2).
To further investigate the mechanism by which menthol inhibits TRPV5 currents, we analyzed single-
channel recordings. Recordings from patches containing a single TRPV5 channel at -100 mV showed that
gating was characterized by openings that occur in bursts (Figure 2a). The single-channel current amplitude
remained unaffected by menthol, as indicated by all-points amplitude histograms of selected current
segments (Figure 2b). In contrast, menthol increased both the frequency and duration of non-conducting
events in a dose-dependent manner. To quantify this effect, we idealized channel openings and compiled
open and closed dwell time histograms (Figure 2c and d). The gating behavior of TRPV5 shows three
exponential components in the closed-time distribution and two components in the open-time distribution
(Table 1 and 2). The number of exponential components in these distributions represents the minimum
number of closed or open states. In this case, data indicates there are three closed or non-conductive states
and one or two open states. These kinetics are consistent with the model in Scheme I (Figure 1g), although
this is not a definitive model.
Further analysis of single-channel recordings shows that menthol induces a concentration-dependent
lengthening of the longer closed-state durations, while reducing the slow component of the open-state
durations, consistent with menthol blocking ion conduction and shortening the length of bursts of openings
(Figure 2e, f and Table 1 and 2). These findings indicate that menthol inhibition occurs via a blocking
mechanism that does not alter single-channel current amplitude, a characteristic feature of slow channel
blockers33.
Structural mechanism of TRPV5 blockade by menthol.
To gain structural insight into the molecular mechanism by which menthol blocks TRPV5, we determined the
cryoEM structure of full-length rabbit TRPV5 in complex with menthol. A priori, it is unclear whether menthol
solely blocks the channel or also induces an alternative conformational state to close the channel. Given
that TRPV5 adopts an open state in the presence of PI(4,5)P , we initiated our experiments with a PIP₂-
2
activated channel and subsequently applied menthol to assess its effect, which are similar conditions to
those in which current recordings are performed. First, purified TRPV5 embedded in lipid nanodiscs was
incubated with 400 μM PI(4,5)P for 45 min to activate the channel, followed by the addition of 1 mM
2
menthol and further incubation for 30 min before vitrification. CryoEM data processing yielded a structure at
3.37 Å resolution in a single conformational state, without imposed symmetry, which we refer to as
TRPV5 , (Supplementary figure 3 and Supplementary table 3).
PIP2+Menthol
The TRPV5 structure reveals a clear density at the intracellular entrance of the pore, positioned
PIP2+Menthol
between the S6 helices, consistent with presence of the menthol molecule (Figure 3a, b). Importantly, this
density was not observed in the previous published TRPV5 structures24,25 (Supplementary figure 4d).
PIP2
The model suggests that one molecule of menthol is primarily coordinated by two W583 residues, forming a
potential hydrogen bond (2.8 Å) between its hydroxyl group and the amide group of W583, as well as a CH-
π interaction (3.3 Å) with the indole ring of the adjacent W583 residue. Notably, W583 has been previously
shown to coordinate the binding of a lysine residue from CaM, which also inhibits TRPV57,34, and to stabilize
the ligand ciss-22a in TRPV635.
Comparing TRPV5 structure with the control structure, TRPV5 in the presence of PI(4,5)P
PIP2+Menthol 2
(TRPV5 )17, we found that the pore remains in a semi-open state (RMSD=0.5 Å) (Figure 3c-i). Specially,
PIP2
the presence of menthol within the pore slightly reduces the pore diameter at I575. This effect is
accompanied by a conformational change in the rotameric angle of W583, which shifts to accommodate
hydrophobic interactions with the ligand. As a result, the pore at W583 adopts a conformation closely
resembling the apo state (Figure 3f). Consistent with this observation, we detected densities at the PI(4,5)P
2
binding site that resemble partially a PI(4,5)P molecule (Supplementary figure 4e). These densities, as
2
previously reported, are in contact with the basic residues R302, R305, K484, and R584, where the
interaction with R584 being one of the most important for inducing the open conformational state12,17,34. Both
our patch-clamp and cryo-EM results suggest that menthol blocks TRPV5 in the open state, a mechanism
like that of CaM, further reinforcing the role of W583 as a key regulatory site for channel modulation.
Menthol binds to W583 in TRPV5 channels.
To functionally validate this interaction, we introduced the W583Q mutation, which removes potential
hydrophobic and aromatic interactions while preserving side-chain size and introducing a polar group. The
W583Q mutation significantly reduced menthol-induced inhibition, shifting the dose-response curve to
higher concentrations (IC = 3.7 mM, Figure 4a and c), indicating that W583 is critical for menthol binding,
50
as suggested by the cryo-EM structure. Single-channel recording confirmed the reduced inhibition by
menthol of this mutant. W583Q channels exhibited distinct gating behavior comparted to WT. Whereas WT
TRPV5 opens in bursts, W583Q channels displayed continuous opening and closing events (Supplementary
Figure 5), similar to the previously reported W583L mutation14. The closed-time distribution contained two
time-constants that remined unaffected by menthol, while the open-time distribution was fitted with two
exponentials components (Supplementary table 1 and 2), consistent with Scheme I, indicating that the
mutations did not greatly alter channel gating. W583Q showed a slight reduction in the slow component with
increasing menthol concentrations. At the highest concentrations, in contrast to WT channels, menthol
reduced the single-channel current amplitude in W583Q, suggesting that in the absence of a tryptophane at
position 583, menthol behaves as a fast blocker, accounting for the remaining block (Supplementary Figure
5d).
Despite this mutation producing a gain-of-function phenotype, shifting channel open probability and the I-V
curve to more positive potentials (Supplementary figure 1 and Supplementary figure 6, respectively),
W583Q retained the inward rectification characteristic of TRPV5 (Figure 4a and Supplementary Figure 6a).
Furthermore, the mutant was also blocked by the pore blocker ruthenium red (RR) with an IC close to that
50
of WT channels, indicating that the mutation does not alter the pore architecture and that its effect is specific
to block by menthol (Supplementary figure 7).
Menthol block was also tested in the previously characterized W583A mutant, for which a cryo EM structure
exists7 (Figure 4b). Similarly to W583Q, W583A showed reduced menthol block (Figure 4b and c). The
observation that both small or large polar substitutions at position W583 greatly impair menthol binding,
supports the importance of hydrophobic interactions in stabilizing menthol binding.
Our cryo-EM structure further suggests that menthol may be stabilized at its binding site through a hydrogen
bond between its hydroxyl group and the indole of W583 (Figure 4d). To test this interaction, we substituted
W583 by a phenylalanine, which lacks an indole group and cannot form hydrogen bonds. The W583F
mutant exhibited a right-shifted menthol dose-response curve, suggesting reduced affinity (Figure 4e, f).
Similarly, W583Y, which retains hydrophobicity but introduces a hydroxyl group, also impaired menthol
block. These results highlight the requirement for specific indole chemistry of tryptophane at position W583
for menthol coordination (Figure 4e, f).
Since many W583 mutation produce gain of function phenotypes (14 and Supplementary figure 6), as control
we introduced mutations at nearby positions. Mutations M578L and G579A, which are localized in the inner
gate and near W583, yielded inwardly rectifying channels with menthol sensitivity similar to WT, confirming
that the effects W583 substitutions on menthol block are specific and not due to gross alteration of pore
structure (Supplementary figure 8). Importantly, G579A has previously been reported to yield stable
macroscopic currents under divalent-free recording conditions14. In the same study, M578 was not identified
as a major contributor to pore constriction, consistent with our observation that the M578L mutation does not
affect menthol sensitivity (Supplementary figure 8).
As presented in the previous section, our structural and functional data reveal that menthol binds to the
intracellular entrance of the TRPV5 pore, specifically interacting with residue W583 while the pore remains
open. To probe the dynamics of menthol pore occupancy, we ran 500 ns all-atom molecular dynamics (MD)
simulations of the open-state TRPV5
PIP2
structure (PDB: 8FFO), with menthol molecules initially placed
randomly in the aqueous phase. Our results showed that the protein stabilized after ~20 ns (RMSD = 2-4 Å,
Supplementary figure 9e), with minor fluctuations (RMSF ~2 Å) observed at the intracellular entrance of the
pore (Supplementary figure 9f), suggesting that the presence of menthol does not induce substantial
conformational changes in the protein. All four simulations replicas showed menthol entering and occupying
the pore from intracellular site (Supplementary figure 9a and b). Trajectory analysis revealed that menthol
molecules can permeate the plasma membrane (Supplementary figure 9d). No Na+ permeation events
occurred during any menthol-occupied state. To quantify the position of menthol relative to the pore, we
measured its distance from I575 (Supplementary figure 9a, b). Unexpectedly, menthol remained at W583 for
only a brief period, forming transient hydrogen bonds lasting 0.1-0.5 ns, before establishing an interaction
with other residues inside the pore, particularly I575, which appeared to stabilize menthol. Once a menthol
occupied the pore, additional menthol molecules interacted more frequently with W583 (Supplementary
figure 9c), suggesting that both W583 and I575 are key residues involved in menthol-mediated TRPV5
blockade.
Effect of mutations at position I575.
To investigate the role of I575 in menthol binding, as suggested by the MD simulations, we tested the I575S
mutant, which should eliminate hydrophobic interactions and introduce a polar residue. This mutation also
diminished menthol inhibition, shifting the dose-response curve to higher concentrations and decreasing the
fraction of blocked current, even at high menthol concentrations (Figure 5a, d, e). The magnitude of this
effect was comparable to that observed in W583Q, suggesting that menthol interacts with I575, or
alternatively, that the presence of a polar residue at position 575 disrupts menthol interactions with W583.
As a control, we tested the I575L mutation, which preserves a hydrophobic residue but could alter sidechain
packing near the protein backbone and should induce little deformation. This mutant retains the menthol
blocking affinity of WT (Figure 5b, d, e). The results indicate that menthol might move from its W583 binding
site to a deeper position within the pore and requires a hydrophobic amino acid at position 575.
Finally, we examined the W583Q-I575S double mutant. These channels remained inwardly rectifying and
retained their affinity for the pore blocker ruthenium red (Supplementary figure 7), indicating that the
combined mutations did not drastically alter TRPV5 gating. However, the double mutant exhibited
significantly reduced susceptibility to menthol inhibition (Figure 5c, d, e), almost completely eliminating block
by menthol, confirming that both W583 and I575 are essential for menthol binding and TRPV5 blockade.

Molecular biology and cell transfection
The gene encoding full-length rabbit TRPV5 (rbTRPV5; UNIPROT id: Q9XSM3·TRPV5_RABIT) ion channel
cloned in pCINeo/IRES-GFP was a gift from Dr. Tibor Rohacs (Rutgers University). This is a bicistronic
plasmid containing both the channel and a GFP (UNIPROT id: Q17105_AEQVI) sequence under separate
promotors, allowing identification of transfected cells by looking for GFP-fluorescent cells. Human TRPV5
(UNIPROT id: Q9NQA5·TRPV5_HUMAN) was subcloned in the pCDNA3.1(+) vector and was a gift from Dr.
Sharona Gordon (University of Washington). TRPV6 (UNIPROT id: Q9H1D0·_HUMAN) was cloned from
human placenta and was donated to us by Dr. Tibor Rohacs54. Residue numbers refer to the human TRPV5
sequence (729 amino acids); the corresponding regions in human TRPV6 (725 aa) and rabbit TRPV5 (730
aa) are conserved, so numbering is the same across all three proteins in this study.
Single and double mutations were introduced into the rbTRPV5 gene using mutagenic oligonucleotides in
whole-plasmid PCR reactions employing KOD Hot Start DNA polymerase (Novagen-Millipore Corp.)
according to the manufacturer's instructions. PCR products were treated with 1 μl DpnI restriction enzyme
(New England Biolabs) and incubated 5 hrs at 37 °C to remove the parent plasmid. The samples were
transformed into DH5α E. coli competent cells. For each mutant, five colonies were picked and inoculated in
5 mL LB medium, and the plasmids were extracted using a home-made miniprep procedure55. Mutants were
confirmed by automatic sequencing.
Plasmids encoding hTRPV5, hTRPV6 and rbTRPV5-IRES-GFP wild-type and with mutations were
transfected into Human Embryonic Kidney 293 (HEK293) cells (ATCC CRL-1573) using the JetPei reagent
(Polyplus Transfection, France) according to the provider's protocol. Cells were maintained in Dulbecco's
modified Eagle's medium (DMEM) (Gibco, Grand Island, NY, USA) supplemented with 10 % fetal bovine
serum and 1 % of antibiotics (penicillin and streptomycin) (Invitrogen USA), at 37°C, in a 5 % CO
2
atmosphere and were reseeded every 3 days using 0.05 % trypsin-ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid
(Trypsin-EDTA) in 35mm culture dishes over glass coverslips for subsequent electrophysiology assays.
Experiments were performed 19–24 hours after transfection with 1 μg of rbTRPV5-IRES-GFP (wild-type or
mutant). Due to the low cell viability observed after expression of most mutants, a separate plasmid
encoding pEGFP-N1 was introduced to enhance the identification of transfected cells. For single-channel
recordings, 25 ng of wild-type or mutant DNA for 24 hours was used, along with 100 ng of the pEGFP-N1
plasmid, to identify transfected cells.
Patch-clamp recording and data analysis
For patch-clamp recordings, transfected cells were identified as green-fluorescing cells using an inverted
microscope (Nikon Ti) with LED-based fluorescence illumination (478 nm excitation, 505 nm dichroic
mirror, 535/40x nm emission filter) and a 40x objective. Macroscopic currents from HEK293 cells expressing
wild-type or mutant channels were obtained in the outside-out configuration, employing the following
divalent-free extracellular (pipette) and intracellular (bath) solutions (in mM): 140 NaCl , 10 EGTA (ethylene
glycol-bis(β aminoethyl ether)-N,N,N′,N′-tetraacetic acid), 10 HEPES (4-(2-hydroxyethyl)−1
piperazineethanesulfonic acid); intracellular (bath); 140 NaCl, 10 EGTA, 10 HEPES, adjusted to pH 7.2 with
NaOH. Menthol or recording solution was applied by placing the outside-out patch in front of a gravity-feed
perfusion system. All chemicals for solutions were acquired from Sigma-Aldrich. Recording pipettes were
pulled from borosilicate capillary glass (Sutter Instruments) using a P-97 puller (Sutter Instruments) and fire
polished to a final resistance in recording solutions of 3-5 MΩ. Currents were elicited by voltage-clamp
pulses from -100 mV to 50 mV of 200 ms duration applied every 3 seconds and monitored for several
minutes during menthol application. Current-voltage (I-V) curves were obtained by changing the membrane
potential in 10 mV steps from -150 to +100 mV (200 ms duration) every 3 seconds at a 0 mV holding
potential.

Due to reduced expression levels of several mutant channels macroscopic currents were recorded in the
whole-cell configuration. On the day of recording, cells were briefly detached using Trypsin-EDTA and
reseeded onto glass coverslips so they did not attach strongly to the glass surface. After obtaining the
whole-cell configuration, cells were lifted and placed in front of the perfusion system for the application of

recorded using the same procedures for WT channels.
Preparation of menthol and ruthenium red solutions
(-)-Menthol was obtained from Santa Cruz Biotechnology, dissolved in absolute ethanol to form a stock
solution at 200 mM, and then diluted from this stock in recording solution at the desired concentration (1 M,
10 M, 100 M, 500 M, 1 mM, 3 mM). These working solutions were then sonicated for 5-10 minutes
before use and prepared fresh for every recording day. The higher concentration of (-)-menthol used (3 mM)
had a final ethanol concentration of 1.5 %, thus, 1.5 % ethanol in recording solution was used as a control in
all experiments after (-)-menthol application and it was determined that it did not affect channel currents.
Ruthenium red (Ammoniated Ruthenium Oxychloride, Sigma-Aldrich) was prepared as a stock solution at
100 M in water. Dilutions where prepared from this stock to reach concentrations of 0.5 nM, 1 nM, 10 nM,
100 nM, 500 nM, 1 M.
Igor Pro 8 software (Wavemetrics) was used for analysis, including fitting, single-channel analyses,
statistical analysis and figure preparation. Data were assumed to follow a normal distribution, and
hypothesis testing was performed using unpaired, two-tailed Student’s t-tests.
TRPV5 protein preparation
TRPV5 preparation and purification followed the protocol described in34. Briefly, the rabbit TRPV5 with a C-
terminal 1D4 epitope tag in a YepM vector 23 was transfected into BJ5457 Saccharomyces cerevisiae
(ATCC) using an alkali-cation yeast transformation kit (MP Biomedicals), according to the instructions of the
manufacturer. Transformed cells were plated on SD-Leu agar plates and allowed to grow at 30°C for 2
days. 30-50 colonies were picked from a plate and inoculated into a single 125 mL starter culture containing
SD-Leu media and 10% v/v glycerol. The culture was incubated at 30°C until reaching the top of the log
phase (OD 1.0–1.4). After confirmation of protein expression by Western blot, the cells were grown at 30°C
with shaking at 200 rpm in 2.5 L of media per flask until OD of 1.0–1.4 was reached. Cells were harvested
by centrifugation at 3000 × g, resuspended in storage buffer (25 mM Tris-HCl, pH 8.0, 300 mM sucrose, and
1 mM PMSF) on ice, and then spun down at 3000 × g to discard the supernatant. Cell pellets were
subsequently stored at −80°C. This expression culture was propagated using 15 mL of the previous growth
at OD 1.0–1.4 for several days until the desired amount was obtained.
Approximately 60 L of growth cells were thawed and resuspended in 300 mL of homogenization buffer (25
mM Tris-HCl, pH 8.0, 300 mM sucrose, 5 mM EDTA, and protease inhibitor cocktail). The resuspended cells
were lysed using a M110Y microfluidizer (Microfluidics) at 100-120 psi. The membranes were separated
from cellular debris by centrifugation at 3,000 × g for 10 min, followed by centrifugation of the supernatant at
14,000 × g for 35 min. The membranes obtained from the previous spin were then pelleted at 100,000 × g
for 1 h. The pelleted membranes were harvested and resuspended on ice using a 15 mL tissue
homogenizer (Kontes Duall with PTFE pestle) in buffer containing 25 mM Tris-HCl, pH 8.0, 300 mM
sucrose, and 1 mM PMSF, and stored at −80°C.
TRPV5 was solubilized from the thawed membranes in solubilization buffer (20 mM HEPES, pH 8.0, 150
mM NaCl, 2 mM TCEP, and 0.87 mM LMNG). The insoluble fraction was separated by centrifugation at
100,000 × g for 1 h. The resulting supernatant was incubated with 1D4-antibody coupled to CnBr-activated
Sepharose beads for 3 h. The beads were collected on a gravity flow column, washed with wash buffer (20
mM HEPES, pH 8.0, 150 mM NaCl, 2 mM TCEP, and 0.064 mM DMNG). The beads were incubated with
elution buffer (20 mM HEPES, pH 8.0, 150 mM NaCl, 2 mM TCEP, and 0.064 mM DMNG, 3 mg/mL 1D4
peptide) overnight. TRPV5 was eluted in 1 mL fractions every 5 minutes. Peak fractions were pooled and
concentrated using a 100-kDa concentrator (Millipore). For reconstitution into nanodiscs, an equimolar
amount of MSP2N2 protein was incubated with the detergent-solubilized TRPV5 in the presence of soy
polar lipids and DMNG detergent in a 1 mL reaction volume. The molar ratio of TRPV5:MSP2N2:lipid:DMNG
in mixture was 1:1:200:500. Lipids and DMNG were dissolved in 20 mM HEPES, pH 8.0, 150 mM NaCl, 2
mM TCEP (SEC buffer). The reaction mixture was incubated on ice for 30 min, followed by the addition of
~30 μL of Bio-Beads. The mixture was rotated at 4°C for 1 h. The supernatant was transferred to a new
tube, and another 30 μL of fresh Bio-Beads was added before rotating at 4°C overnight to complete the
reaction. Reconstituted TRPV5 was subjected to a Superose 6 increase 10/300 GL column (GE Healthcare)
equilibrated with SEC buffer. Fractions containing nanodisc reconstituted TRPV5 were pooled and
concentrated to 2.57 mg/ml.
Cryo-EM sample preparation and data collection
TRPV5 sample was incubated with 400 μM diC8-PI(4,5)P (Echelon Biosciences, Cat# P-4508) for
PIP2+Menthol 2
45 minutes and 1 mM Menthol (Sigma-Aldrich, Cat# 2216-51-5) for 30 minutes, corresponding to a 1:53:132
(TRPV5:PIP2:Menthol) molar ratio. Menthol was solubilized in 100% ethanol (200 mM) and then diluted at
15% in SEC buffer (30 mM). Final sample contained 1% ethanol. 3 μL TRPV5 sample was applied
PIP2+Menthol
to glow-discharged 1.2/1.3 Quantifoil Holey Carbon Grids (Quantifoil Micro Tools) using a Vitrobot Mark IV
(Thermo Scientific). The sample was blotted in a chamber at 4°C and 100% humidity for 6 s at 0 blotting
force before being freezing in liquid ethane.
Samples were imaged on a Titan Krios G3i 300 kV electron microscope with a Gatan K3 direct electron
detector. 40-42 frame movies were collected with a nominal dose of 41-43 e−/Å2. Super-resolution images
for all datasets were collected at 105,000 magnification with a pixel size of 0.415 Å/pixel.
Data processing
Two datasets of 5,427 (DSA) and 4,736 (DSB) movies were collected and processed in cryoSPARC
v4.4.158,59. Movies were patch motion corrected with a Fourier-crop factor of 0.5 and an alignment resolution
of 3 Å, followed by the patch CTF estimation. Micrographs were manually curated based on a maximum
CTF fit resolution of 8 Å. The template for autopicking were created with 94,896 (DSA) and 94,858 (DSB)
particles blob picked from subsets of 300 micrographs from each dataset and used for extraction. 1,281,269
and 1,491,899 particles were extracted and binned by a factor of 4 with a box size of 72 pixels from DSA
and DSB, respectively. These particles were 2D classified with 100 classes, resulting in 360,885 (DSA) and
225,211 (DSB) good particles that were re-extracted. A three-class heterogeneous refinement was
performed to separate good particles with the TRPV5 apo map (EMD-25716
[https://www.ebi.ac.uk/emdb/EMD-25716]) as a reference, resulting in a good class of 233,564 (DSA)
and 160,664 (DSB) particles at 0.83 and 1.66 Å/pix, respectively. Particles were refined with a non-uniform
refinement with no symmetry to generate the initial model12. Particles from DSA were subjected to 3D
classification with 5 classes focusing on the pore region. The best class, totaling 57,516 particles, were
combined to produce a map with a resolution of 3.53 Å with no symmetry at 0.83 Å/pix. These particles were
subjected to two rounds of heterogeneous refinement and non-uniform refinement, resulting in 33,086
particles, which produced a structure with a resolution of 3.44 Å. Similarly, 22,633 particles were obtained
from DSB after subjected to two rounds of heterogeneous refinement and non-uniform refinement: these
particles generated a structure with a resolution of 3.83 Å. Both datasets were combined and
heterogeneously refined into three volumes. The best structure form with 42.348 particles was refined with a
non-uniform refinement to produce the final map with a resolution of 3.37 Å with no symmetry.
The local resolution was determined in cryoSPARC, and the angular distributions were generated with the
UCSF pyem package.
Model building
The TRPV5 model (8FFO [https://doi.org/10.2210/pdb8FFO/pdb]) (Lee et al. 2023) was used as the
PIP2
initial model and manually adjusted in ISOLDE60. Lipids, PI(4,5)P (PIO), and Menthol (IT9), obtained from
2
the ePDB database, were docked and manually adjusted in COOT61. Real Space_Refinement and eLBOW
from the PHENIX software62 were used to refine and to generate ligand restraints, respectively.
Pore profiles were determined using HOLE63. Chimera, ChimeraX, and PyMol were used for analysis,
visualization and figure generation.
Molecular dynamics simulations
The TRPV5 coordinate model (PDB ID: 8FFO [https://doi.org/10.2210/pdb8FFO/pdb]) (Lee et al. 2023),
PIP₂
oriented using the 6DMU structure from the Positioning of Proteins in Membranes (OPM) server
(http://opm.phar.umich.edu/server.php), was embedded in a 1-palmitoyl-2-oleoyl-sn-glycerol-3-
phosphocholine (POPC) lipid bilayer (606 molecules) along with phosphatidylinositol-4,5-bisphosphate
(model with PIO, 4 molecules) and ergosterol (8 molecules) at pH 7.3. The protein-membrane complex was
solvated with TIP3 water, 100 mM NaCl, and approximately 8 mM menthol, resulting in a system containing
84,087 water molecules, 203 Na⁺, 151 Cl⁻, and 20 menthol molecules within a 160 × 160 × 160 Å³
simulation box (Supplementary Table 4). The membrane-protein system was built using the CHARMM-GUI
membrane builder65 (http://www.charmm-gui.org). The topologies for menthol and PIO were generated
using CGenFF server (https://cgenff.com, Supplementary information), then converted from CHARMM
CGenFF toppar stream files to GROMACS format using cgenff_charmm2gmx_py3_nx2.py
(https://mackerell.umaryland.edu/charmm_ff.shtml) together with the charmm36-jul2022.ff force field
(https://mackerell.umaryland.edu/charmm_ff.shtml). Menthol molecules were placed randomly in the
aqueous region.
Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations were performed using the GPU-accelerated GROMACS 2024.366
package with the CHARMM36m force field67. The system was energy-minimized and equilibrated using the
steepest descent algorithm in CHARMM-GUI without modifications in configuration files (Supplementary
information). In the final equilibration step, the system remained stable with a total energy of −2.75 × 10⁶ ±
691.63 kJ/mol, where the potential energy was −3.76 × 10⁶ ± 1340.85 kJ/mol and the kinetic energy was
1.01 × 10⁶ ± 1171.37 kJ/mol. The temperature remained at 303.18 ± 0.35 K, and the volume at 3631.97 ±
1.17 nm³. The protein RMSD remained at 0.058 ± 0.008 nm. The temperature was maintained at 303 K
using a Nosé−Hoover thermostat, and the pressure at 1 bar using a Parrinello−Rahman barostat. Bond
constraints were applied using the LINCS algorithm. Long-range electrostatic interactions were calculated
using the Particle Mesh Ewald (PME) method with a 12 Å cutoff and updated every 2 fs. Van der Waals
interactions were switched at 10 Å with a 12 Å cutoff. Production simulations consisted of four independent
500 ns runs at 0 mV membrane voltage, and trajectory analyses were performed using GROMACS tools
and VMD.
Molecular docking
Docking of menthol into the cryoEM structure was carried out with AutoDock Vina implemented in
SwisDock68. We used a box of 18 x 18 x 8 Å comprising the position of W583. Default parameters were
used with an exhaustivity of 64.
Data availability
All cryo-EM data generated in these studies are available upon request from Vera Y. Moiseenkova-Bell
(vmb@pennmedicine.upenn.edu). The cryo-EM maps have been deposited in the Electron Microscopy Data
Bank (EMDB) under accession code EMD-70173 [https://www.ebi.ac.uk/pdbe/entry/emdb/EMD-70173]
(TRPV5 ); EMD-25716 [https://www.ebi.ac.uk/em db/EMD-25716] (TRPV5 ); EMD-29049
PIP2+Menthol Apo
[https://www.ebi.ac.uk/emdb/EMD-29049] (TRPV5 ). The atomic coordinates have been deposited in the
PIP2
Protein Data Bank (PDB) under accession code 9O6G [https://doi.org/10.2210/pdb9O6G/pdb]
(TRPV5 ); 8TF2 [https://doi.org/10.2210/pdb8TF2/pdb] (TRPV5 ): 8FFO
PIP2+Menthol Apo
[https://doi.org/10.2210/pdb8FFO/pdb] (TRPV5 ). All molecular dynamics trajectories can be accessed on
PIP2
Zenodo [https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.18472580]69. All other data is included in the paper. Source data are
provided with this paper.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
This study by Méndez-Reséndiz and colleagues reports that menthol is an inhibitor of the Ca-selective TRP channel
TRPV5. Using macroscopic and single-channel recordings, the authors first find that menthol inhibits in a manner that is
consistent with it being a slow channel blocker. The authors then collect cryo-EM images of rabbit TRPV5 in the presence of
menthol and PI(4,5)P2, resolving a single structure in which a small non-protein density is observed near the intracellular
entrance of the pore, where it could act as a pore blocker. This non-protein density is assigned as menthol as it was not
observed in previous reconstructions of TRPV5 in the absence of menthol. The modelled menthol interacts with the side
chains of W583 from each protomer. In contrast to the pose observed in the cryo-EM analysis, Molecular dynamics
simulations suggested that menthol binds primarily near I575. Electrophysiological analysis of mutant channels indicated
that some mutations to I575 and W583 can disrupt menthol binding. Although the finding menthol
can inhibit TRPV5 is
intriguing, the evidence supporting the proposed mechanism of inhibition is insufficient for publication.
Comments.
1. It is not clear that the features are sufficiently well resolved in the cryo-EM map made available to the reviewers to model
the interactions between TRPV5 and menthol. The densities corresponding to W583, which are proposed to interact with
menthol, are poorly resolved, limiting the authors ability to precisely model their positions. The density for the putative
menthol is similarly poorly resolved. Collectively, these features limit the authors ability to determine how menthol binds with
the channel. Higher quality reconstructions in which the side chains and menthol can be precisely modelled would greatly
strengthen this study. This is especially critical as the MD simulations are not in agreement with the binding pose observed
in the cryo-EM map.
2. As a technical question, what besides the menthol drives the asymmetry of the reconstruction such the menthol can be
modelled in a single pose in which it interacts uniquely with each of the four TRPV5 protomers. The methods did not
describe the use of symmetry expansion, which might aid in defining any asymmetry in the channel-menthol complex.
3. It is surprising that the menthol is so dynamic in the simulations when it appears to be stably bound in the cryo-EM map.
Also, it preferentially binds to residues such as I575 and G579. These interactions do not agree with the cryo-EM analysis,
where a single pose is resolved for menthol bound to W583. It is difficult to reconcile the findings of the two approaches.
4. Menthol is proposed to act a channel blocker. Was channel activity evaluated during the MD
simulations? Does menthol
effectively block ion permeation in all of the observed poses? What is the effect of membrane potential in MD simulations?
The macroscopic recordings appear to indicate that the menthol block is not voltage dependent. A more detailed evaluation
of the effect of menthol on ion permeation would be helpful in elucidating the mechanism of inhibition.
5. The lack of agreement between the cryo-EM analysis and the MD simulations makes it difficult to interpret the
mutagenesis. The authors show that menthol is a less potent inhibitor of the I575S and W583Q mutants, as well as the
I575S/W583Q double mutant. However, these mutations alter the hydrophobicity and surface potential of the pore. The
authors indicate that at least one of these mutants alters channel properties as well. The effects of alternative substitutions at
these positions should be tested to better understand the role of I575 and W583 in channel function and menthol binding. It
is also important to examine other residues near the intracellular gate that are not predicted to interact with menthol.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
The study by Mendez-Resendiz and De Jesus-Perez et al. investigates the TRPV5 ion channel, a member of the transient
receptor potential (TRP) vanilloid family, and identifies menthol as an inhibitor. This research integrates functional data
obtained through electrophysiology experiments with structural data from cryo-electron microscopy, and validates binding
sites via mutagenesis and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations.
Overall the paper is well written and interesting, although it is not quite clear to me in its current form how far beyond the
TRP(V) family the general interest of these findings will extend since a clear introduction to the motivation (and potential
physiological role) of menthol as a TRPV5 inhibitor is currently missing. That said, I think the paper is publishable after
clarification of a few details:
Most importantly, the motivation behind testing menthol as a modulator for TRPV5 function should be elaborated on.
Additionally, any physiological context where menthol inhibition of TRPV5 could be relevant, particularly in the kidney,
should be discussed. Understanding the rationale behind this study extends beyond developing a pharmacological
compound to its broader implications. Furthermore, the introduction lacks the comparison to previous studies looking at
menthol as a modulator of e.g. TRPV1 and TRPV3 activity. This becomes more pertinent as these channels lack the central
tryptophan residue identified here for TRPV5 to be crucial for menthol binding.
Material and Methods :
Please specify UniProt or NCBI identifiers for the protein/genes used.
Material methods, line 200, please specify if these are molar ratios. Material methods, line 207. Please indicate the molar
ratios between TRPV5, PIP2, and menthol in your sample preparation. Also, please specify the buffer solutions that your
respective additives were dissolved in.
For cryo-EM sample preparation, it looks as if you went right for a menthol/PIP2 bound co-complex structure, but you do not
actually clarify in the introduction the role of PIP2 on TRPV5. So it would be nice to add a couple of sentences on the role of
PIP2 for TRPV5 activity and why you decided to determine a co-structure rather than a TRPV5 menthol only structure.
I am unclear about the starting structure(s) of the MD simulation, because currently it reads as if you had only used the prior
structure of Lee et al of PIP2-bound TRPV5, which were then adjusted by adding menthol to the simulation. However, what
about your newly determined structure in the presence of menthol and PIP2? Is the menthol bound state stable in
simulations using your own cryoEM structure as a starting model?
Please indicate all equations used for fits (especially referring to Fig 2/S1), either in the material methods or in the
supplementary section. Line 459, where is this equation of tau (menthol) and the numbers used therein coming from?
Result/Discussion
Fig 1/Supplementary Figure 1 shows clear differences for human TRPV5 and V6 compared to rabbit V5, e.g. Hill coefficient
of ~0.5 and ~1, respectively. A Hill coefficient of <1 indicates negative cooperativity, while the nH of ~1 for rabbit V5 is in
agreement with the shared binding site in the cryoEM data. This would suggest fundamentally different interaction and/or
regulation across channels and species. Could you please clarify your models for menthol binding and functional regulation
compared between the three proteins? Furthermore, maybe the authors could have another look at the quality of the fits in
the supplementary figure and try out different binding models, it seems the current fits are not ideal.
In the patch clamp experiments, menthol was added from the outside, but the binding site in the channel seen by EM is on
the cytosolic side. Figure 3H places menthol in a solvent channel but interacting with 4 Trp residues. Can the authors please
add a few sentences about diffusion of menthol across bilayers and hydrophobicity of this molecule? This is interesting
because menthol is considered to be relatively hydrophobic, but the binding site looks as if it would be accessible from the
solvent phase.
Do the contacts drawn in Fig 3G for the menthol hydroxy group reflect the stabilizing contacts of this molecule? It seems
likely that rather than with the indole ring moiety, the OH group might form an H-bond with the NH group of the Trp sidechain
placed “above” the menthol? The authors may also possibly better illustrate the hydrophobicity of the binding pocket by a
space filling model of both side chain and ligand, but that is just for demonstration purposes.
Menthol is an asymmetric molecule, interacting with a (presumably) symmetric homotetramer. I feel the authors have missed
an opportunity to maybe discuss the putatively imposed asymmetry by a ligand in a little more depth.
The van der Wijst lab has previously proposed that the tryptophan residue is also important for ion coordination (see e.g.
https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1820323116), is menthol inhibition/binding altered in the presence of higher cation
concentrations? Furthermore, a W/A mutation shows a gain of function phenotype, it looks as if the W/Q mutant used here
also has this effect, but this is not explicitly mentioned in the text. This could potentially be interesting as glutamine, in
contrast to alanine, should retain some ion complexation ability? So does this mean that cation complexation at this site is
not important for channel regulation?
I wonder whether the W/Q mutant shows a similar or a more restrained GOF effect than the W/A mutant described in the
literature. Can the authors comment on why they chose the W/Q mutant?
Results around Figure 2: It is interesting that the authors find three time constants for menthol concentration-dependent
closure of the channel. Can the authors speculate what these time constants actually reflect on a molecular level? And is the
change in the differences in tau shown in Figure 2E as the yellow and the blue traces actually in any way significant for the
inhibition model the authors propose (as these seem to not significantly change with the ligand concentration)?
MD simulations: How different is the orientation of the Ile and Trp chains identified here for menthol binding between the
starting structure by Lee et al and your own cryoEM structure? How mobile are these residues when menthol is present vs
when it is not bound?
With MD you find 2 possible menthol binding sites, is there any density at all at the “upper” site in the cryoEM maps? And
what is the chemical nature of the contacts observed for menthol in the two binding sites in the MD simulations? Related to
this, if the contacts between menthol and TRPV5 stem from solely from hydrophobic interactions with the Trp and Ile
residues, how is there any specificity for menthol at this site?
Does mutation of W/Q or I/S in silico shift the menthol occupancy to the respective “other” binding site? This is a relatively
straightforward experiment that would strengthen the relevance of the two binding sites (see also next point):
What was the rationale behind creating an Ile to Ser mutation? I575 is a pore constriction residue in TRPV5, so wouldn’t it
be expected that loss of this hydrophobic residue results in loss of menthol block? This may just reflect a more open pore,
but does not necessarily mean this residue is in direct contact with menthol, something that the lack in electron density for
this site also alludes to?
Minor points:
Throughout the introduction, residue numbers are mentioned, presumably following human nomenclature, but possibly also
rabbit as this is the channel used for this study? This needs specification as the introduction discusses TRPV5 channels
broadly and does not distinguish between species.
Figure 2, it may be my PDF version, but the quality, especially of figure 2A, is quite poor. There are boxes around the plot.
Maybe the authors could check that.
Legend Figure 2E and F: I have stumbled a little bit over the phrasing, “the dependence of the three…” (in E) and
“dependence of the two time constants” (in F). It would help to really clearly write (in the main text and/or the legend)
which time constants you are referring to here, respectively.
Line 456, spelling mistake in ‘concentration’.
Detail the preparation of the menthol solution in Ephys experiments, including concentration, solvents used and which
controls were used (it’s not clear to me whether the control was just buffer or contained ethanol?).
For legends of figures showing Ephys data, specify that this involves TRPV5 in Hek293 cells.
Although a prior structure of TRPV5 with PIP2 exists, the authors should at least briefly describe the lipid binding site(s) they
see in their cryoEM structure in the main text. Do menthol and PIP2 binding affect each other in any way?
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
In the work of A. Mendez-Resendiz et al. based on data from electrophysiological experiments, determination of the spatial
structure of the TRPV5 channel by cryo-EM, point mutagenesis, and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, it was concluded
that menthol blocks the protein in the open state. A menthol binding site formed by W583 residues has been identified in the
lower gate of the channel. It has been suggested that W583 is involved in menthol-mediated TRPV5 inhibition. Given the
significant physiological role of this class of channels, the presence of pathological conditions caused by disorders in their
work, as well as the relatively small number of their known inhibitors, the topic seems relevant, and the results are necessary
both for understanding the physical foundations of action of the TRP channels and for the rational design of new
pharmacological agents and therapies. At the same time, the interpretation of some crucial data presented in the paper, a
number of arguments of the authors in their favor, as well as the conclusions drawn, raise serious questions and doubts for
me, which does not allow, in my opinion, to publish the work in its present form.
The main critical points are listed below.
Since the methods and approaches used by the authors are currently quite routine, including in relation to the study of TRPV
channels, the scientific novelty of the work lies only in the identification of a new inhibitor of the TRPV5 channel in the open
state - menthol molecules. The evidence presented by the authors in favor of this hypothesis raises the following questions:
1. The attribution of the density observed in the region of W583 in the cryo-EM model to the menthol molecule is not justified.
Thus, the menthol arrangement shown in Fig. 3g relative to the four W583 residues does not reveal the presence of specific
and strong intermolecular interactions. In particular, the OH group of menthol is directed towards the nearest 6-membered
ring of indole (the distance is 3.3 A, although it is unclear between which atoms), while the methyl group of menthol forms an
unfavorable contact with the NH group of the indole ring. etc. It can be assumed that MD results reflect the instability of this
ligand arrangement - the population of such MD-states is significantly lower than a number of alternative states near
residues I575, A576 and G579. At the same time, the presence of additional electron density in these areas is not observed
in cryo-EM. This also contradicts with the phrase on page 13: “…as the I575S and W583Q-I575S mutations drastically
reduced the potency of menthol blocking, indicating that menthol dynamically interacts with these two residues”. In addition,
since the channel narrows in the I575 region, it is quite expected that menthol molecules will be located in this place, since
their size does not allow for free diffusion, at least considering the pore radius (Fig. 3f) and the size of menthol. But the
authors do not discuss these important issues.
2. It is well known (see the reference Van Der Wijst (2017) and other sources, e.g., DOI: 10.1073/pnas.1820323116) that
point mutations of W583 can seriously affect the functional characteristics of the channel, therefore, the changes observed
by the authors in the effect of menthol on the conductivity parameters may be due to a whole set of factors, from which the
role of menthol needs to be isolated. It seems to be a difficult task, which has not been completely solved in this work.
I believe that the conclusions drawn in this case are based on an overly simplified picture.
Other comments.
- It is unclear exactly how the 20 menthol molecules were positioned in the initial MD configurations - the authors only
mention that “menthol molecules were placed randomly in the aquatic region of the intracellular compartment”. However,
it should be borne in mind that nonpolar menthol molecules can effectively interact with the protein residues closest to them,
locking themselves in these positions and not reaching the entrance to the channel. However, according to the authors'
results (Fig. S4, b), at least 10 menthol molecules were detected in the pore, between residues I575 and W583. How is such
selectivity achieved?
- Parameterization of the force field for the menthol molecule was performed using an automated service, without the
necessary calibration on simple model systems. Since menthol is poorly soluble in water, the effects of oligomerization in a
polar environment are possible – these issues need to be clarified in order to understand how adequate the MD results are.
- When processing the experimental dose-response curves (Fig. 2 c, d; Fig. 4 d, e), the measured profiles are fitted with
several gaussians, although this is not justified in any way. As a result, such a decomposition in many cases looks incorrect
and, accordingly, distorts the conclusions.
- Page 10: “The single-channel current amplitude remained unaffected by menthol, as indicated by all-points amplitude
histograms of selected current segments (Figure 2b)”. But the histograms are rather different… Moreover, they are different
from those reported for WT TRPV5 in (DOI: 10.1038/srep45489) (Fig. 2f). But these effects are not discussed.
- The curves in Figure S1 c, e do not reach a plateau, how in this case the Hill coefficient can be estimated?
It is unclear exactly what information is needed to understand the conclusions provided by the graphs of RMSF versus MD
time (Figure S4, f)? The authors remarked that such plots reveal “minor fluctuations (~2 Å) observed at the intracellular
entrance of the pore” (page 11). But what was the reason to report the whole RMSF plots without discussing them?
- Page 12: The meaning of the following phrase is not clear to me: “…in the absence of a tryptophane at position 583,
menthol blocks TRPV5 by rapidly entering and exiting the conduction pathway, albeit with lower affinity”.

peer_review_rounds.author_response:
We thank the reviewers for insightful and constructive comments. We have carried out most of
the suggested changes and answered all the comments included in the three reviews. These
include changes to the manuscript text, new analysis and new experiments. We think that these
changes provide further support for menthol being a pore blocker primarily binding to residue
W583. The manuscript has been strengthened, and we have clarified several sections of it. Below
we provide a point-by-point answer to the reviewers’ comments. Our individual answers are
written in blue text and we have indicated new and changed text in our revised manuscript in
green highlight.
Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
This study by Méndez-Reséndiz and colleagues reports that menthol is an inhibitor of the Ca-
selective TRP channel TRPV5. Using macroscopic and single-channel recordings, the authors
first find that menthol inhibits in a manner that is consistent with it being a slow channel blocker.
The authors then collect cryo-EM images of rabbit TRPV5 in the presence of menthol and
PI(4,5)P2, resolving a single structure in which a small non-protein density is observed near the
intracellular entrance of the pore, where it could act as a pore blocker. This non-protein density is
assigned as menthol as it was not observed in previous reconstructions of TRPV5 in the absence
of menthol. The modelled menthol interacts with the side chains of W583 from each protomer. In
contrast to the pose observed in the cryo-EM analysis, Molecular dynamics simulations suggested
that menthol binds primarily near I575. Electrophysiological analysis of mutant channels indicated
that some mutations to I575 and W583 can disrupt menthol binding. Although the finding menthol
can inhibit TRPV5 is intriguing, the evidence supporting the proposed mechanism of inhibition is
insufficient for publication.
Comments.
1. It is not clear that the features are sufficiently well resolved in the cryo-EM map made available
to the reviewers to model the interactions between TRPV5 and menthol. The densities
corresponding to W583, which are proposed to interact with menthol, are poorly resolved, limiting
the authors ability to precisely model their positions. The density for the putative menthol is
similarly poorly resolved. Collectively, these features limit the authors ability to determine how
menthol binds with the channel. Higher quality reconstructions in which the side chains and
menthol can be precisely modelled would greatly strengthen this study. This is especially critical
as the MD simulations are not in agreement with the binding pose observed in the cryo-EM map.
We sincerely thank the reviewer for their thoughtful and constructive evaluation of our cryo-EM
data and proposed menthol binding site.
As correctly noted, the density corresponding to W583 side chains and the putative menthol ligand
is not resolved at a level that permits precise atomic modelling of side-chain conformations or
unambiguous placement of the ligand. We believe that the limited resolution around W583 is not
incidental, but rather a consequence of the dynamic nature of menthol binding and its
predominantly hydrophobic interactions. Menthol is a small, hydrophobic molecule that does not
engage in strong, directional interactions and is unlikely to strongly contact W583 residues from
every subunit simultaneously. As such, it does not sufficiently anchor the surrounding residues to
enable accurate modelling of their side-chain conformations. Furthermore, we emphasize that our
cryo-EM map was refined without imposing symmetry, which may reduce the accuracy of
averaged density in this region.
Despite these limitations, we observe a reproducible non-protein density at the intracellular
entrance of the pore. This density is absent in control structures and is consistent in size and
shape with that of menthol, supporting its interpretation as menthol occupancy. Given the
proximity of this density to W583 and the established functional role of W583 in CaM binding, we
propose this as a plausible, albeit not definitive, orientation of menthol within the binding site.
Upon re-evaluation of our data, we observed that menthol may adopt an alternative pose in which
the hydroxyl group of menthol forms a potential hydrogen bond (2.8 Å) with the amide group of
W583, and a CH-π interaction may occur with the indole ring of an adjacent W583 residue (3.3
Å). This prompted us to generate and test the W583F mutant, which retains the aromatic π surface
required for hydrophobic CH–π contacts but eliminates the indole N–H hydrogen-bond donor
unique to tryptophan. As expected, W583F displayed a reduced menthol effect, supporting a
model in which menthol engages W583 through both π-mediated hydrophobic interactions and a
specific hydrogen bond to the indole N–H. Similarly, the newly analysed W583Y mutant maintains
an aromatic ring and has a hydroxyl group, but this hydroxyl group cannot replace the indole N–
H hydrogen bond present in tryptophan, leading to a similar reduction in menthol’s effect (Figure
4d-f).
While our molecular dynamics simulations indicate that menthol does remain bound to W583,
there are also transient contacts are observed with I575, a residue identified through MD as
shaping a hydrophobic region and facilitating ligand accommodation. This interpretation is
supported by our mutagenesis experiments, which show that both I575S and W583Q mutations
significantly reduce menthol-mediated inhibition, indicating that both residues contribute to
menthol’s functional modulation of TRPV5.
Regarding the molecular dynamics simulations, these were conducted independently of the cryo-
EM model to explore the dynamics of menthol-channel interactions. While the simulations suggest
alternative poses and transient interactions with W583, we interpret these as complementary to,
rather than contradictory of, the cryo-EM data. The differences between the experimentally
observed density and the MD-derived poses likely reflect the limitations of both approaches,
including obtaining the structure in its most stable state and the inherent approximations and
timescale constraints of MD simulations.
2. As a technical question, what besides the menthol drives the asymmetry of the reconstruction
such the menthol can be modelled in a single pose in which it interacts uniquely with each of the
four TRPV5 protomers. The methods did not describe the use of symmetry expansion, which
might aid in defining any asymmetry in the channel-menthol complex.
As suggested, we did perform symmetry expansion on the final reconstructed map to investigate
potential asymmetries in menthol binding. However, using this approach did not improve the
resolution or clarify additional features related to ligand binding. Specifically, the symmetry-
expanded particles did not yield better-defined density for menthol or reveal distinct binding poses
across the four protomers.
Given these results, we opted to proceed with the conventional (non-symmetry-expanded)
reconstruction strategy, which provided the most interpretable and reliable density for the
complex. However, as indicated in our response to the previous question, reprocessing of our
data suggest specific interactions in which menthol may adopt an alternative pose in which the
hydroxyl group of menthol forms a potential hydrogen bond (2.8 Å) with the amide group of
W583, and a CH-π interaction may occur with the indole ring of an adjacent W583 residue (3.3
Å) (Figure
3g and Figure 4d-f).
3. It is surprising that the menthol is so dynamic in the simulations when it appears to be stably
bound in the cryo-EM map. Also, it preferentially binds to residues such as I575 and G579. These
interactions do not agree with the cryo-EM analysis, where a single pose is resolved for menthol
bound to W583. It is difficult to reconcile the findings of the two approaches.
We thank the reviewer for raising this important point. We cannot say categorically that cryoEM
result and MD simulation are not in agreement, but rather, MD gives us additional information
about the dynamics of the blocking process. Our cryo-EM data identify W583 as the principal
menthol-binding site, while the MD simulations provide complementary information by suggesting
a second, transient interaction near I575. This additional site may be relevant for understanding
the electrophysiological recordings, as it reflects the dynamic nature of menthol binding and its
relationship to the narrow part of the pore. We also note that the experimental conditions for MD,
cryo-EM, and electrophysiology differ which likely contributes to the apparent discrepancies.
Unfortunately, were not able to solve the structure for this second site, but we observed a density
at this position in a subset of particles, although these were not sufficient to achieve high
resolution (Figure R2). Taken together, we interpret the MD as an approach that complements
the structural and functional data, with W583 representing the main binding site and I575
contributing to a more dynamic, secondary interaction.
As mentioned above, we acknowledge that there are some factors that may help explain the
apparent discrepancies in menthol binding between the experimental results and our simulations:
First, Force-field limitations for menthol. Menthol parameters were generated using the CHARMM
General Force Field (CGenFF). Although slightly penalties were reported during
parameterization, subtle inaccuracies in partial charges or dihedral potentials may reduce the
fidelity of menthol’s interactions in our system. For example, the dipole moment calculated in a
system with menthol and solution results ~2.1 D, a value slightly higher than published previously
(1.4 D)1.
Differences in experimental versus simulation conditions. Prior to vitrification, the protein was
incubated at 4 °C with diC8-PI(4,5)P₂ and menthol for 30 minutes, whereas in our MD simulations
the system was held at 29.8 °C for 500 ns. This temperature difference corresponds to an
estimated menthol diffusivity of ~3.7 × 10⁻¹⁰ m²/s at 4 °C versus ~8 × 10⁻¹⁰ m²/s at 29.8 °C. As a
result, over a 100-ns trajectory, menthol would sample on average ~4.7 nm at 4 °C and ~7 nm at
29.8 °C, increasing its likelihood of exploring alternative binding poses in silico. Furthermore, our
simulations (∼500 ns) are short relative to the timescales over which experimental equilibrium is
achieved. We therefore cannot rule out that menthol might converge on the single W583 pose at
longer timescales or under different sampling strategies.
Despite these caveats, our MD results have been instrumental in guiding mutagenesis
experiments, as mutations at residues highlighted by the simulations produced the largest shifts
in TRPV5’s menthol sensitivity, corroborating the biological relevance of our computational
predictions. For example, although MD suggested that menthol may form transient contacts with
I575 in the narrow part of the pore, no defined density was observed at this site in our cryo-EM
maps. Consistently, the I575S mutation abolished menthol inhibition, most likely due to disruption
of the local hydrophobic environment rather than loss of a specific binding interaction, whereas
the I575L mutation preserved inhibition, indicating that a large hydrophobic side chain at this
position is sufficient to maintain pore properties.Together, these results suggest that I575 shapes
the hydrophobic context of the pore but may not constitute a primary menthol-binding determinant,
which is more clearly supported by the cryo-EM density and mutagenesis at W583. A comparable
mechanism has been described for tetra-butyl ammonium (TBA) block of hERG K+ channels,
where the blocker first binds to an aromatic residue in the cavity and then moves further up the
pore to interact with a narrowing isoleucine site2 (discussion, page 10, lines 284-286).
4. Menthol is proposed to act a channel blocker. Was channel activity evaluated during the MD
simulations? Does menthol effectively block ion permeation in all of the observed poses? What is
the effect of membrane potential in MD simulations? The macroscopic recordings appear to
indicate that the menthol block is not voltage dependent. A more detailed evaluation of the effect
of menthol on ion permeation would be helpful in elucidating the mechanism of inhibition.
Yes, we monitored ion flux throughout the molecular dynamics simulations to assess the impact
of menthol on channel conduction. Under the conditions simulated, no ion permeation events
were observed. While Na⁺ ions were consistently present and coordinated within the selectivity
filter and lower vestibule (Figure S9), they did not possess sufficient energy to traverse the lower
gate of the channel.
This absence of conduction is expected given the lack of a driving force in our setup. Specifically,
the simulations were performed under symmetric NaCl concentrations and at 0 mV membrane
potential. Therefore, we chose not to introduce a transmembrane potential in the simulation in
order to focus on spontaneous binding and occupancy under equilibrium-like conditions.
Importantly, when menthol occupied the pore, particularly in the position near I575, it effectively
occluded the conduction pathway. Although some water molecules were able to pass through, no
ion flux was detected, supporting the notion of a physical block. These observations are consistent
with menthol acting as a pore blocker and help to illustrate its inhibitory mechanism, even in the
absence of transmembrane voltage.
We have now clarified these aspects in the revised Results sections to better highlight the
functional interpretation of the MD simulations in the context of our electrophysiological data
(Results, page 8, lines 218-233).
Furthermore, in response to the reviewer comment, we performed two replicas of MD simulation
applying a voltage of −400 mV for 200 ns to determine the effect of membrane potential on TRPV5
in the presence of menthol. As in our previous simulations without voltage, Na⁺ could enter the
pore and reach its vestibule from the extracellular side (distance region >0 in the Figure R1).
However, no ions crossed the conduction path before menthol entered from the intracellular side.
Likewise, some cations accessed the pore from the intracellular side (distance region <0), but
none passed through, either because the electric field direction was unfavourable or because
menthol was already blocking the pore.
Figure R1. Distances of menthol molecules or sodium ions from the center of mass of I575 were
measured in two MD simulations of 200 ns each, applying a voltage of –400 mV. Negative values
indicate that molecule occupies the pore from the intracellular side. Dashed lines indicate the
center of mass of I575 and W583. In both simulations, menthol occupied the pore (blue),
remaining at I575 as observed in the simulations without voltage. Similarly, Na⁺ was able to enter
the pore, more frequently from the extracellular side; however, no permeation events were
observed.
In addition, we thank the reviewer for raising the point about the voltage dependence of channel
block by menthol. To address this, we analysed our data to estimate the voltage dependence of
the fraction of blocked current at three menthol concentrations. This analysis shows that menthol
block is indeed slightly voltage dependent. This result was intriguing since menthol is a neutral
molecule and the identified binding site lies outside the membrane electric field, making a classical
Woodhull mechanism unlikely3. However, the observed voltage dependence can be explained by
a model in which the channel opens after transitions between two closed states and becomes
blocked only in the open state. The voltage dependence of block arises from the fact that opening
is voltage-dependent and thus blocking is coupled to channel opening. This linear model, based
on van der Wijst et al.4, was further constrained by measuring the voltage dependence of the
channel opening In single-channel recordings (Supplementary fig S1). The model accounts for
both the dose dependence and the observed voltage dependence of menthol block. We have
included this data in a new Figure 1 to clarify the mechanism of channel block by menthol and its
effect on ion permeation, as suggested by the reviewer (Page 4, lines 102-111). Model details are
presented in an appendix. We have also carried out a characterization of the effect of high
concentration of permeant ions (300 mM Na+) on the blocking effect of menthol, as suggested by
reviewer 2. The result of these experiments indicates that the fraction of current blocked by
menthol remains the same for control (140 mM Na+) and high Na+, suggesting that menthol does
not compete for a permeant ion binding site (see Figure R2).

5. The lack of agreement between the cryo-EM analysis and the MD simulations makes it difficult
interpret the mutagenesis. The authors show that menthol is a less potent inhibitor of the I575S
and W583Q mutants, as well as the I575S/W583Q double mutant. However, these mutations alter
the hydrophobicity and surface potential of the pore. The authors indicate that at least one of
these mutants alters channel properties as well. The effects of alternative substitutions at these
positions should be tested to better understand the role of I575 and W583 in channel function and
menthol binding. It is also important to examine other residues near the intracellular gate that are
not predicted to interact with menthol.
We appreciate the reviewer’s insightful comments regarding the interpretation of our mutagenesis
data in the context of the cryo-EM and MD results. We agree that cryo-EM provides a static picture
whereas MD highlights the dynamic nature of menthol binding, suggesting transient interactions
not only with W583, but also with I575 in the narrow part of the pore. Although no defined density
was observed at I575 in the cryo-EM maps, the I575S and I575L mutants help clarify its role: the
loss of menthol inhibition in I575S is most likely due to disruption of the local hydrophobic
environment rather than elimination of a specific menthol contact, while preservation of block in
I575L supports the importance of maintaining a hydrophobic side chain at this constriction. By
contrast, W583 emerges as the primary determinant of menthol binding, as supported by cryo-
EM density, MD, and mutagenesis. Substitution of W583 with either phenylalanine or tyrosine
retained aromaticity but impaired menthol block, demonstrating that the indole NH group and
extended π-surface unique to tryptophan are essential (Figure 4 and page 7, lines 197-204).
To address the reviewer’s concern about nonspecific effects, we have now introduced mutations
at neighboring residues (G579A and M578L) that are not predicted to interact with menthol. Both
mutants behaved very similarly to wild type and did not alter menthol block, supporting the
specificity of W583 as a binding site (Supplementary figure 8). Furthermore, electropysiology
confirmed that all mutants preserved the general channel properties, including conductance–
voltage relationships, inward rectification, and blok by ruthenium red, indicating that the observed
effects are not due to a disruption of pore function (Supplementary figures 6 and 7).
Together, these results resolve the apparent differences between cryo-EM and MD by showing
that menthol binding is dynamic, with W583 as the principal site and I575 contributing to the
hydrophobic environment of the pore, while control mutations confirm that the effects are not
attributable to nonspecific pore alterations.
Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
The study by Mendez-Resendiz and De Jesus-Perez et al. investigates the TRPV5 ion channel,
a member of the transient receptor potential (TRP) vanilloid family, and identifies menthol as an
inhibitor. This research integrates functional data obtained through electrophysiology experiments
with structural data from cryo-electron microscopy, and validates binding sites via mutagenesis
and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations.
Overall the paper is well written and interesting, although it is not quite clear to me in its current
form how far beyond the TRP(V) family the general interest of these findings will extend since a
clear introduction to the motivation (and potential physiological role) of menthol as a TRPV5
inhibitor is currently missing. That said, I think the paper is publishable after clarification of a few
details:
Most importantly, the motivation behind testing menthol as a modulator for TRPV5 function should
be elaborated on. Additionally, any physiological context where menthol inhibition of TRPV5 could
be relevant, particularly in the kidney, should be discussed. Understanding the rationale behind
this study extends beyond developing a pharmacological compound to its broader implications.
Furthermore, the introduction lacks the comparison to previous studies looking at menthol as a
modulator of e.g. TRPV1 and TRPV3 activity. This becomes more pertinent as these channels
lack the central tryptophan residue identified here for TRPV5 to be crucial for menthol binding.
We agree with the reviewer that the rationale for this study extends beyond compound
development and lies in understanding how a monoterpene such as menthol differentially
modulates members of the TRP family. Menthol is a well-established activator of TRPM8, an
agonist of TRPV3, and exerts inhibitory effects on TRPV1 and TRPV4, even though these
channels lack the central tryptophan residue that we identify here in TRPV5. This comparison
highlights the novelty of our work: while menthol’s effects on TRPV1 and TRPV3 involve residues
in the S4–S5 linker, our results demonstrate that in TRPV5 menthol interacts with W583 at the
lower gate to function as a slow pore blocker. Thus, our findings uncover a structurally distinct
and channel-specific mechanism that broadens the understanding of how menthol can exert both
agonist and inhibitory actions across the TRP channel family. We have now better argued the
rationale behind our study and improved the presentation regarding the possible physiological
implications of menthol block of TRPV5 channels in the introduction (page 3, lines 76-83). We
have also moved mention of menthol effects on other TRP channels from the discussion to the
introduction as requested (page 3) and improved the discussion of these findings (page 9, lines
259-269).
In addition, we have expanded the Discussion to explicitly address menthol’s effects on other
TRP channels and to emphasize this conclusion.
