Our simulations were designed to explore the process of menthol binding and its potential
mechanism of channel blockade. In line with the rationale behind our experimental design, where
purified TRPV5 was incubated with PI(4,5)P₂, to open the channel, and menthol, we aimed to
capture spontaneous binding events in silico. To this end, and given the extensive computational
resources required to achieve relevant simulation timescales (~15 ns/day on our setup), we
initiated simulations using the previously published structure of TRPV5 bound to PI(4,5)P₂ 6, while
our cryo-EM data were still being processed.
Because the menthol binding site was unknown a priori, menthol molecules were placed randomly
in the solvent at locations sufficiently distant from the protein to avoid introducing bias in their
positioning. This allowed us to observe spontaneous interactions and possible binding pathways
without constraining the ligand to a predefined pose.

after transient binding to W583 or deeper sites such as I575, we predict that starting from our own
structure would not have significantly altered the outcomes. As discussed previously, this dynamic
behavior is likely influenced by a combination of factors, including menthol’s hydrophobic nature,
the absence of a strong anchoring site, and limitations in the ligand parameterization.

physically possible for it to cross from the outside to the inside of the plasma membrane of cells7.

Thank you, we admit that we did not clearly explain the results of the single

interpreted as the channel visiting at least three closed states. This is consistent with the gating
scheme I we now use to explain the menthol data, presented in figure 1. The two fastest time
constants likely correspond to the transitions between closed states labelled C1 and C2 and the
third one, which is the slowest, corresponds to the blocked state.
MD simulations: How different is the orientation of the Ile and Trp chains identified here for
menthol binding between the starting structure by Lee et al and your own cryoEM structure?
How mobile are these residues when menthol is present vs when it is not bound?
In Figure 3g, we compare the structure of TRPV5 in the presence of menthol and PIP₂ to the
structure with PI(4,5)P₂ alone. We find that the I575 residues do not exhibit significant positional
differences, primarily because the S6 helix backbone remains unaltered. In contrast, the W583
side chains of two subunits shift their orientation by approximately 20° to 45° to accommodate
menthol binding.
To address the reviewer’s question regarding the evolution of residue orientation, we calculated
the side-chain angle of isoleucine and tryptophan relative to the plane formed by the Cα atoms of
each residue across four MD replicas (as shown in the figure R2). The periods during which
menthol resides in the pore are highlighted in pink. Overall, the orientation of I575 and W583 does
not appear to be directly correlated with the presence or absence of menthol. However, it is
interesting to note that in run 1, a single menthol molecule seems to induce continuous variation
in I575 orientation (ranging from 10° to 80°), while the presence of multiple menthol molecules
(after ~350 ns) appears to stabilize the side-chain conformation (~50°). A similar trend is observed
in run 3, which also shows increased stabilization (~50°), likely due to multiple menthol molecules
being present. Conversely, in these same runs, the orientation of W583 becomes more dynamic
in the presence of more than one menthol molecule, fluctuating between 25° and 80°.
Figure R2. Side-chain angle (red dash line) of isoleucine (a) and tryptophan (b) relative to the plane
formed by the Cα atoms of each residue across four MD replicas. Pink region indicates pore occupancy
by menthol, as showed in Supplementary Figure S9.
With MD you find 2 possible menthol binding sites, is there any density at all at the “upper” site in
the cryoEM maps? And what is the chemical nature of the contacts observed for menthol in the
two binding sites in the MD simulations? Related to this, if the contacts between menthol and
TRPV5 stem from solely from hydrophobic interactions with the Trp and Ile
residues, how is there any specificity for menthol at this site
While our current cryoEM structure does not reveal clear density near I575 (Figure R3a, right),
we identified a subset of particles that display additional non-protein density near this region in a
locally refined reconstruction (Figure R3a, left, red circle). This map, obtained at ~3.8 Å resolution,
suggests the possibility of menthol binding at the "upper" site, albeit with greater conformational
heterogeneity. We acknowledge, however, that this density is low-resolution and should be
interpreted with caution.
In our MD simulations, the interactions between menthol and I575 appear to be primarily
hydrophobic in nature. Interestingly, we also observe transient hydrogen-bond interactions
between menthol and W583 (0.1–0.5 ns; Figure R3b, red diamonds) as the molecule traverses
the pore. These interactions suggest that the donor/acceptor functional group of menthol can form
a hydrogen bond with the NH group of W583. This transient but specific hydrogen bonding may
contribute to selectivity beyond simple hydrophobic contacts. Therefore, although hydrophobic
interactions dominate, the ability of menthol to engage in polar interactions with specific residues
such as W583 may help explain its preferential binding at these sites.
Figure R3. a. Comparison of cryoEM structures shown in Figure 3 (right) and the ~3.8 Å reconstruction
obtained from a subset of particles displaying additional non-protein density in the pore (left, red circle).
b. Transient hydrogen-bond interactions (red diamonds) between menthol and W583 obtained in our
MD simulation.
Does mutation of W/Q or I/S in silico shift the menthol occupancy to the respective “other” binding
site? This is a relatively straightforward experiment that would strengthen the relevance of the
two binding sites (see also next point):
We thank the reviewer for this suggestion. Unfortunately, the computational power and time
required to perform such simulations exceed the resources currently available to us, and we are
therefore unable to obtain sufficient sampling to unequivocally determine whether the W/Q or I/S
mutations shift menthol occupancy to an alternative binding site. This is an important point
because, even without performing in silico experiments on occupancy shifts, our
electrophysiological data are in agreement with the MD results showing that I575 is an important
site influencing menthol block, which is interesting given that it represents the narrowest part of
the pore and preserves, as the reviewer mentioned, the hydrophobicity of the pore. The lack of
electron density in this region suggests that binding is dynamic; moreover, we performed two
mutations at this site: substitution with is polar and serine, which strongly decreased the block
effect, and substitution with leucine, which completely preserved the block. Importantly, other
mutants at nearby positions previously reported to affect channel gating (M578L and G579L) had
no effect on menthol block (Supplementary figure 8), supporting the idea that I575 plays a
transitory role in menthol block.
What was the rationale behind creating an Ile to Ser mutation? I575 is a pore constriction residue
in TRPV5, so wouldn’t it be expected that loss of this hydrophobic residue results in loss of
menthol block? This may just reflect a more open pore, but does not necessarily mean this residue
is in direct contact with menthol, something that the lack in electron density for this site also
alludes to?
Our rationale for introducing the I575S mutation was to test whether reducing hydrophobicity and
side-chain volume at this pore-constriction residue alters menthol block. As the reviewer notes,
I575 is located at the narrowest part of the TRPV5 pore, and replacing this bulky hydrophobic
side chain with a smaller polar residue is indeed expected to affect pore geometry and
conductance. Consistent with this, I575S reduced menthol sensitivity, an effect that can be
explained by changes in local pore architecture and hydrophobicity, while the absence of electron
density for menthol at this site suggests that binding here may be dynamic or transient. To further
clarify this, we also examined the I575L mutant, which preserves hydrophobicity at this position,
and found that it retained WT-like block, whereas neighbouring substitutions (M578L and G579L)
did not affect block. Importantly, I575S reduced menthol sensitivity without altering overall channel
conductance (Supplementary Fig. S6), or the sensitivity to ruthenium red block, supporting the
idea that hydrophobic interactions at the pore constriction contribute to menthol’s blocking effect.
Taken together, we interpret the I575S and I575L results as complementary to W583Q,
suggesting that residues at or near the pore constriction influence the ability of menthol to access
and transiently occupy the conduction pathway, while W583 plays a central role in mediating the
specific blocking interaction.
Minor points:
Throughout the introduction, residue numbers are mentioned, presumably following human
nomenclature, but possibly also rabbit as this is the channel used for this study? This needs
specification as the introduction discusses TRPV5 channels broadly and does not distinguish
between species.
We thank the reviewer for this observation. Human TRPV6 contains 725 amino acids, human
TRPV5 contains 729, and rabbit TRPV5 contains 730; however, these differences are confined
to the C-terminus. As a result, the amino acid numbering is conserved across all three proteins.
We have now clarified this point in the Methods section (page 12, lines 349-351).
Figure 2, it may be my PDF version, but the quality, especially of figure 2A, is quite poor. There
are boxes around the plot. Maybe the authors could check that.
Thanks for pointing this out, it seems the boxes were introduced during pdf conversion, in the
current revision we have fixed these errors.
Legend Figure 2E and F: I have stumbled a little bit over the phrasing, “the dependence of the
three…” (in E) and “dependence of the two time constants” (in F). It would help to really clearly
write (in the main text and/or the legend) which time constants you are referring to here,
respectively.
We thank the reviewer for pointing this out. We have revised the legend (and corresponding text)
to clearly specify which time constants are shown. In Figure 2E we now write “dependence of the
three closed-time constants (Table Ia)", and in Figure 2F “dependence of the two open-time
constants (Table Ib).
Line 456, spelling mistake in ‘concentration’.
Fixed
Detail the preparation of the menthol solution in Ephys experiments, including concentration,
solvents used and which controls were used (it’s not clear to me whether the control was just
buffer or contained ethanol?).
Thanks for pointing this out. Menthol was prepared as a 200 mM stock solution in absolute
ethanol. From this solution, the adequate dilution in recording solution was prepared. These
dilutions were then sonicated 10 min and used immediately. The control was recording solution
containing ethanol at the maximum concentration used, which was 1.5 % and corresponded to
the ethanol content of the 3 mM menthol solution. We have now included these details in the
Methods section (page 14, lines 421-427). Also, figures indicate the application of 1.5 % ethanol
at the beginning of the recordings
For legends of figures showing Ephys data, specify that this involves TRPV5 in Hek293 cells.
Although a prior structure of TRPV5 with PIP2 exists, the authors should at least briefly describe
the lipid binding site(s) they see in their cryoEM structure in the main text. Do menthol and PIP2
binding affect each other in any way?
We now specify in the figure legends that the recordings were obtained from rabbit TRPV5
expressed in HEK293 cells, and we have added a brief description of the PIP₂ binding site:
“Consistent with this observation, we detected densities at the PI(4,5)P₂ binding site that resemble
a PI(4,5)P₂ molecule (Supplementary Figure 3e). These densities, as previously reported, are in
contact with the basic residues R302, R305, K484, and R584, where the interaction with R584
being one of the most important for inducing the open conformational state.”
Regarding the second question: Unlike the effect of the pore blocker Ruthenium Red or the
inhibitor econazole, which induce conformational changes in the channel pore, mediated by
interactions with N574 in the former case and W495 in the latter, menthol appears to obstruct
physically the ion permeation pathway without inducing any evident conformational changes.
Therefore, we conclude that menthol does not affect PI(4,5)P₂ binding.
Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
In the work of A. Mendez-Resendiz et al. based on data from electrophysiological experiments,
determination of the spatial structure of the TRPV5 channel by cryo-EM, point mutagenesis, and
molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, it was concluded that menthol blocks the protein in the
open state. A menthol binding site formed by W583 residues has been identified in the lower gate
of the channel. It has been suggested that W583 is involved in menthol-mediated TRPV5
inhibition. Given the significant physiological role of this class of channels, the presence of
pathological conditions caused by disorders in their work, as well as the relatively small number
of their known inhibitors, the topic seems relevant, and the results are necessary both for
understanding the physical foundations of action of the TRP channels and for the rational design of
new pharmacological agents and therapies. At the same time, the interpretation of some crucial
data presented in the paper, a number of arguments of the authors in their favor, as well as the
conclusions drawn, raise serious questions and doubts for me, which does not allow, in my
opinion, to publish the work in its present form.
The main critical points are listed below.
Since the methods and approaches used by the authors are currently quite routine, including in
relation to the study of TRPV channels, the scientific novelty of the work lies only in the
identification of a new inhibitor of the TRPV5 channel in the open state - menthol molecules. The
evidence presented by the authors in favor of this hypothesis raises the following questions:
1. The attribution of the density observed in the region of W583 in the cryo-EM model to the
menthol molecule is not justified. Thus, the menthol arrangement shown in Fig. 3g relative to the
four W583 residues does not reveal the presence of specific and strong intermolecular
interactions. In particular, the OH group of menthol is directed towards the nearest 6-membered
ring of indole (the distance is 3.3 A, although it is unclear between which atoms), while the methyl
group of menthol forms an unfavorable contact with the NH group of the indole ring. etc. It can be
assumed that MD results reflect the instability of this ligand arrangement - the population of such
MD-states is significantly lower than a number of alternative states near residues I575, A576 and
G579. At the same time, the presence of additional electron density in these areas is not observed
in cryo-EM. This also contradicts with the phrase on page 13: “…as the I575S and W583Q-I575S
mutations drastically reduced the potency of menthol blocking, indicating that menthol
dynamically interacts with these two residues”. In addition, since the channel narrows in the I575
region, it is quite expected that menthol molecules will be located in this place, since their size
does not allow for free diffusion, at least considering the pore radius (Fig. 3f) and the size of
menthol. But the authors do not discuss these important issues.
We respectfully disagree with the reviewer’s interpretation regarding the assignment of the non-
protein density near W583 as menthol. To evaluate whether this density corresponds to menthol,
we directly compared our cryo-EM reconstruction of TRPV5 in the presence of PI(4,5)P₂ and
menthol with a control dataset obtained under identical conditions but without menthol (Figure
S4d). The control map, as well as other previously published TRPV5 structures in the presence
of PI(4,5)P₂ alone, did not show any comparable non-protein density in this region. Furthermore,
our functional data support the involvement of W583 in menthol sensitivity, providing an
orthogonal line of evidence for the physiological relevance of this site.
As noted, our MD simulations reveal that menthol displays considerable mobility within the pore,
transitioning between an initial binding pose near W583 and a seemingly more stable site near
I575. This expected dynamic behavior complicates definitive assignment of a single binding pose,
but reflects a potential multi-site binding mechanism, where menthol may transiently engage with
W583 before moving deeper into the pore. The observed high mobility is consistent with menthol’s
hydrophobic and dynamic nature.
It is important to mention that we have reevaluated the pose of menthol in light of the reviewer’s
concerns. In the refined conformation, the hydroxyl group of menthol may interact via hydrogen
bonding with the NH group of W583, while a CH–π interaction with the indole ring of a neighboring
W583 side chain may further stabilize its position. Whereas these contacts may not reflect
classical strong polar interactions, they are consistent with the types of interactions expected for
hydrophobic ligands in similar environments. Notably, analogous CH–π interactions have been
observed in previous TRPV5 structures, such as in the case of econazole bound to W49512.
Importantly, new data included in this revised manuscript, obtained from W583F and W583Y
mutants, further support these specific interactions between menthol and W583 (Figure 4).
As the reviewer correctly notes, while our current cryoEM structure did not show a density near
the I575, MD simulations complement that result suggesting that in a dynamic system, alternative
poses near I575, A576, and G579 may be more frequently sampled. Although we did not resolve
high-resolution density in these regions, we identified a subset of particles displaying additional
non-protein density near I575, suggesting that this region may also accommodate menthol, albeit
with lower occupancy or greater conformational heterogeneity (Figure R1a, left). These findings
are supported by functional data: the W583Q mutation partially reduces menthol sensitivity as
well as I575S, and W583Q/I575S double mutant shows a more pronounced effect, indicating that
W583 may play a role in capturing menthol at the pore entrance, while I575 may contribute to
stabilizing it in a deeper, occluding position.
Figure R1. a. Comparison of cryoEM structures shown in Figure 3 (right) and the ~3.8 Å reconstruction
obtained from a subset of particles displaying additional non-protein density in the pore (left, red circle).
b. Transient hydrogen-bond interactions (red diamonds) between menthol and W583 obtained in our
MD simulation.
2. It is well known (see the reference Van Der Wijst (2017) and other sources, e.g., DOI:
10.1073/pnas.1820323116) that point mutations of W583 can seriously affect the functional
characteristics of the channel, therefore, the changes observed by the authors in the effect of
menthol on the conductivity parameters may be due to a whole set of factors, from which the role
of menthol needs to be isolated. It seems to be a difficult task, which has not been completely
solved in this work. I believe that the conclusions drawn in this case are based on an overly
simplified picture.
We appreciate the reviewer’s concern regarding the separation of the gating effects of mutations
and their effect on channel block by menthol. Our data as well as that of Van Der Wijst (2017)
and other sources13, indeed show that there are effects of these mutations on channel gating.
These mutations tend to be gain of function, increasing the channel-mediated current at positive
potentials; we have now measured current-voltage (I-V) curves for all the mutants employed in
this study and confirm that most of them produce a shift towards more positive potentials, which
means that the channels open with less hyperpolarization (Supplementary figure 6). Given that
menthol is an open channel blocker, one would expect an increased occupancy of menthol and
thus an increased blocked fraction at the same open probability. However, we observed a reduced
efficacy of menthol, which can be better explained by mutations reducing the affinity of menthol
to its binding site. In order to evaluate the degree that mutans affect the functionality of the
channel, we have measured in all the mutants the block by ruthenium red (RR) which is also a
pore blocker, whose binding site is located near the selectivity filter. Our data show that the
mutants did not greatly affect block by RR and thus suggest that their effect on menthol is specific,
and the result of disruptions of the binding site (Supplementary figure 7) and not drastic changes
in the functionality of the channel.
- It is unclear exactly how the 20 menthol molecules were positioned in the initial MD
configurations - the authors only mention that “menthol molecules were placed randomly in the
aquatic region of the intracellular compartment”. However, it should be borne in mind that
nonpolar menthol molecules can effectively interact with the protein residues closest to them,
locking themselves in these positions and not reaching the entrance to the channel. However,
according to the authors' results (Fig. S4, b), at least 10 menthol molecules were detected in the
pore, between residues I575 and W583. How is such selectivity achieved?”
We thank the reviewer for pointing out this oversight. The correct statement should be: “Menthol
molecules were placed randomly in the aqueous region.”
In our simulations, menthol molecules were randomly distributed in the bulk solvent on both the
intracellular and extracellular sides of the membrane, ensuring that none were initially in direct
contact with the protein surface or embedded in the lipid bilayer. This setup was chosen to allow
menthol to explore potential binding sites spontaneously during the simulation, without biasing
the outcome.
As the reviewer correctly noted, nonpolar menthol molecules can transiently interact with nearby
protein residues upon initial diffusion, and indeed, we observed frequent but short-lived
interactions between menthol and various surface-exposed residues. However, these interactions
were generally unstable and did not result in persistent occupancy. For example, Figure S4d
shows the diffusion profiles of several menthol molecules along the z-axis, where most remain in
the solvent phase (0–60 Å and 100–160 Å), exhibiting highly disordered motion. In a few
instances, such as the highlighted trajectory of one menthol molecule (light green), the ligand
adopts a seemingly stable pose within the ARD region (~30 Å, Figure S4d) for an extended period
(~350–500 ns).
The observed enrichment of menthol in the pore region, particularly between W583 and I575,
appears to be primarily driven by hydrophobic partitioning. The inner pore of TRPV5 is notably
hydrophobic, providing a favorable environment for menthol binding (Figure S3f). Also, using a
relatively high menthol concentration (~8 mM) increases the likelihood of capturing such events
within the accessible simulation timescales. Nevertheless, menthol occupancy remained variable
across independent runs: for instance, in run 2, only two menthol molecules entered the pore,
one remaining for ~300 ns and the other for ~100 ns; in run 4, a single molecule occupied the
pore transiently for less than 200 ns.
These findings underscore the dynamic occupancy nature of menthol binding under our
simulation conditions, which aligns with its small, hydrophobic character and supports a model in
which menthol acts as a fast pore blocker rather than a tightly bound ligand.
- Parameterization of the force field for the menthol molecule was performed using an automated
service, without the necessary calibration on simple model systems. Since menthol is poorly
soluble in water, the effects of oligomerization in a polar environment are possible – these issues
need to be clarified in order to understand how adequate the MD results are.”
We thank the reviewer for raising this important point. We employed a generalized force field
parameterization menthol using the CHARMM General Force Field (CGenFF), following an
approach similar to that used in previous simulation studies involving menthol using another FF14.
While this method is widely used in molecular simulations, we acknowledge that automated
parameterization without further calibration against high-level quantum mechanical data or
experimental observables may introduce limitations.
In our case, the CGenFF parameterization yielded a parameter penalty score of 0.000 and a
charge penalty of 0.452, values that fall well below the recommended threshold for further
optimization (penalty <10), suggesting acceptable reliability. Nevertheless, we recognize that
even small deviations in partial charges or torsional potential can impact on the behavior of small,
dynamic ligands like menthol in complex environments. For example, our 200-ns test simulation
of menthol in aqueous solution indicated structural stability (RMSD ~1.5 Å), yet the computed
dipole moment (~2.1 D) was slightly higher than previously reported computational estimates
(~1.4 D)15. This deviation may influence menthol’s interaction profile with the pore and
surrounding residues, possibly contributing to the observed differences between our simulation
results and the cryo-EM structure.
Despite these limitations, it is noteworthy that both our structural and simulation data consistently
indicate that menthol occupies the intracellular entry of the pore, and that mutations at key
residues support a model in which it acts as a channel blocker.
Regarding the possibility of menthol oligomerization, we did not frequently observe such behavior
in our simulations. Figure R2 shows the lifetime of oligomerization across four replicas, with a
mean lifetime of 0.26 ± 0.1 ns. This short oligomerization lifetime is likely because menthol
predominantly localizes within the membrane, at the membrane–solution interface, or in contact
Figure R2. Lifetime of oligomerization across four replicas. The mean lifetime is 0.26 ± 0.1 ns.
with the protein, where hydrophobic partitioning limits its self-association in bulk solvent. This
sumulation indicates that formation of menthol complexes is short lived and not relevant for the
interpretation of our results.
- When processing the experimental dose-response curves (Fig. 2 c, d; Fig. 4 d, e), the measured
profiles are fitted with several gaussians, although this is not justified in any way. As a result, such
a decomposition in many cases looks incorrect and, accordingly, distorts the conclusions.
We are sorry for the confusion. The dose responses are obtained from macroscopic current
recordings and are calculated as the fraction of current blocked at a given concentration of
menthol. These estimate does not involve fitting of gaussians. Gaussian functions were fitted to
the amplitude distribution of single-channel records to estimate the possible effect of menthol on
the current amplitude flowing through a single channel. This is necessary to distinguish between
fast block and slow block mechanisms, as a fast blocker will reduce the current amplitude, while
a slow blocker increases the number of non-conducting events. This seems to be the case for
menthol as indicated by the kinetic analysis (figure 2 c-f).
- Page 10: “The single-channel current amplitude remained unaffected by menthol, as indicated
by all-points amplitude histograms of selected current segments (Figure 2b)”. But the histograms
are rather different… Moreover, they are different from those reported for WT TRPV5 in (DOI:
10.1038/srep45489) (Fig. 2f). But these effects are not discussed.
We thank the reviewer for this observation. In Figure 2b, the all-points amplitude histograms
indeed differ in appearance across conditions. This variation is primarily due to changes in
channel open probability with increasing menthol concentrations, which alter the relative
proportion of open versus closed events. In addition, differences in the number of events available
at each concentration affect the shape of the histograms. Despite these changes in overall profile,
the position of the open-state peak relative to the closed-state peak remains constant, indicating
that the unitary current amplitude is unaffected by menthol.
We acknowledge that our histograms also differ in appearance from those reported in the cited
study (DOI: 10.1038/srep45489). This discrepancy is explained by the different recording
conditions: their single-channel currents were measured at –80 mV, whereas ours were acquired
at –100 mV, leading to proportionally larger amplitudes under our conditions.
- The curves in Figure S1 c, e do not reach a plateau, how in this case the Hill coefficient can be
estimated?
Thank you for this insightful observation. We have reanalyzed the dose response curves for
hTRPV5 and hTRPV6 channels. Specifically, the leak current was estimated and subtracted from
the records. We realized that this step is important specially for small amplitude currents.
Application of this correction yielded steeper dose response curves that can be well fitted to a Hill
equation. We also fitted these data to a specific blocking model (Scheme I), which provides a
good fit to the data. Please note that this is now supplementary figure 2. The detailed derivation
of equations used for this model is presented in a new appendix.
It is unclear exactly what information is needed to understand the conclusions provided by the
graphs of RMSF versus MD time (Figure S4, f)? The authors remarked that such plots reveal
“minor fluctuations (~2 Å) observed at the intracellular entrance of the pore” (page 11). But what
was the reason to report the whole RMSF plots without discussing them?
We thank the reviewer for this observation. Root mean square fluctuation (RMSF) analysis
provides insight into the flexibility and mobility of individual residues within a molecular system
throughout the simulation. Regions with high RMSF values typically correspond to flexible
segments such as loops, termini, or intrinsically disordered regions, while low RMSF values are
indicative of more rigid structural elements, including α-helices, β-sheets, or domains engaged in
stable interactions. In our study, RMSF was used to evaluate whether the presence of menthol
induces any local destabilization or increased flexibility, particularly in the pore region of the
channel. As shown in Figure S4f, the average RMSF values remain relatively low (~2 Å) across
the transmembrane region, including the residues lining the pore and those interacting with
PI(4,5)P . These results indicate that the pore remains structurally stable throughout the
2
simulations and that menthol binding does not induce significant conformational changes in this
region.
- Page 12: The meaning of the following phrase is not clear to me: “…in the absence of a
tryptophane at position 583, menthol blocks TRPV5 by rapidly entering and exiting the conduction
pathway, albeit with lower affinity”.
We thank the reviewer for pointing out the lack of clarity. What we intended to convey is that, in
the absence of tryptophan at position 583, menthol can still interact with the pore but with reduced
stability, resulting in rapid entry and exit from the conduction pathway and therefore a lower
apparent affinity for block. We have revised the sentence on page 6, lines 183-185 to read: “In
the absence of tryptophan at position 583, menthol behaves as a fast blocker, accounting for the
remaining block.”

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1: The authors have greatly improved the manuscript and it is now suitable for publication.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
I would like to thank the authors for their patience and the extensive comments to my previous remarks, that have been
answered satisfactorily. The addition of the W583F and Y mutants and the extended data and discussion of the W/A and
W/Q mutants significantly strengthen the manuscript. While I am still not sure I fully understand the physiological relevance
of the menthol interaction with TRPV5, the authors may have come across an interesting druggable pocket in TRPV5, but

The authors have tried to address all the queries expressed in my review. It is important that the corrected version of the
article contains new experimental structural data obtained as a result of additional analysis. The final picture, especially in
terms of matching the experimental and simulation data, became clearer to me.
At the same time, these clarifications and additions to the MD protocol and the interpretation of the simulation results are
present only in the reviewers' responses, but are practically not reflected in the revised version of the manuscript. In
particular, this is related to evaluating the reproducibility of the calculation results, the approximations made, possible
inaccuracies in the selection of the force field, etc. Since the final conclusions of the work on the molecular mechanism of
menthol channel block are largely based on modeling data, I think it is important for the Reader to understand the limitations
of the computational modeling.
A short section could be devoted to this, for example, in the Supporting Information. This is often used in computational
works, which makes it possible to evaluate the predictive power of in silico models. This is especially true since there are
some obvious contradictions between, for example, cryo-EM and MD results – this was noticed by all the referees. In
addition, the “Data and code availability” section does not contain information about the details of calculations - MD
protocols, exact force field parameters (including those for ions), etc. The availability of such data would allow the authors'
results to be used by other researchers in independent calculations of TRPV5 and other systems.

peer_review_rounds.author_response:
We thank the reviewer for the assessment of our manuscript and the previous constructive comments.
We fully agree with the inference that loss of function of TRPV5 has clear and well documented
consequences in renal physiology. TRPV5 is the major apical Ca2+ entry pathway in the distal nephron, and
reduced TRPV5 activity leads to decreased Ca2+ reabsorption, hypercalciuria, and increased risk of renal
stone formation.
In this regard, identifying menthol as a TRPV5 inhibitor does not suggest any therapeutic value for menthol
in renal disease, however, the indiscriminate use of menthol in vaping products or high-menthol exposure
may represent a potential health risk. This is because TRPV5 plays a key role in Ca2+ reabsorption, and its
inhibition at elevated menthol concentrations could disturb Ca2+ handling in the kidney. For these reasons,
TRPV5 inhibition remains biologically meaningful, even though it is not desirable as a therapeutic strategy
for kidney function.
However, the impact of TRPV5 inhibiton may differ substantially in non-renal contexts, particularly in cancer.
Dysregulation of TRPV5/6 has also been associated with disrupted Ca²⁺ homeostasis, increased migration,
and altered growth signaling in renal cell carcinoma and other malignancies (DOI:
10.1016/j.juro.2011.07.086; DOI: 10.1371/journal.pone.0195844). These observations suggest that
inhibition of TRPV5/6 may be of potential therapetic use in cancer biology.
In relation to the second question, defects in TRPV5-mediated Ca2+ reabsorption such as kidney stones or
bone density reduction due to malfunctioning osteoclasts, are related to impaired plasma membrane
trafficking of the channel and not to channels that are unable to open
(https://doi.org/10.1016/j.kint.2019.05.029). It thus seems like what’s needed is not a channel agonist, since
channel opening is not impaired but drugs that can restore trafficking to the plasma membrane. We have
added a paragraph with at the end of the discussion section (lines 338-342).
At this moment, it is not obvious to us how a channel opener could be developed from a molecule that
blocks and stabilizes a closed conformation.
Some additional minor points:
Line 79 – TRPV5 not TRV5
Thanks for pointing this out, we have corrected the typo.
Line 80ff “Menthol also activates or inhibits other TRP channels, such as TRPV3, TRPV1 and TRPA1, 80
although the structural mechanisms involved are not known (Macpherson et al. 2006; Nguyen et al. 81
2021) (Takaishi et al. 2016) (Kashio et al. 2024), although TRPV5 and TRPV6 are only 30 % similar 82 to
other TRPVs suggesting different mechanisms of modulation.” Is not a complete sentence?
Thanks for pointing this mistake out, we have corrected the sentence.
Line 125 - In this case, data indicates there are three closed or non-conductive states and one or two open
states. These kinetics are consistent with the model in Scheme I.
Technically the data can be fitted satisfactorily with 5 states, but that doesn’t mean that there are only 5?
That is correct, the number of fitted states only provides an estimate of the minimum number of states.
More systematic experiments and rigorous examination of alternative models would be needed to obtain a
reliable estimate of the number of states and allowed transitions involved on TRPV5 channel gating. We
have added this statement in line 119.
Line 262 “This property makes menthol is a molecule of physiological interest.” – not a complete sentence
Thanks for pointing this mistake out, we have corrected the sentence.
Line 329 – TRPM8 not TRM8
Thanks for pointing this out, we have corrected the typo.
Line 333 – what is a “high dose exposure” of menthol? This may be mentioned explicitly to allow the reader
to assess the relationship between the IC50 of menthol for TRPV5 and TRPM8, and the possibility of kidney
pathophysiology
Experimental models show that menthol produces biological effects in the hundreds of micromolar to
millimolar concentration range. For example, menthol causes renal proximal tubular cell toxicity at 200–
1500 µM (DOI: 10.1124/jpet.414.129161abstract) and disrupts pulmonary epithelial and mitochondrial
function in a similar range (DOI: 10.1152/ajplung.00222.2022). Toxicological work indicates that adverse
effects appear at very high exposures, such as dietary concentrations of 24-50 mM. Although the
corresponding plasma menthol concentration is unknown. Together, these data indicate that TRPV5
inhibition by menthol occurs only at concentrations that already overlap with doses known to produce
cellular or tissue injury.
We have included this value in line 325.
Regarding the TRP channel pharmacology, menthol activates TRPM8 with an EC50 of 62.6 µM (DOI:
10.3389/fphar.2022.898670), while in our study menthol inhibited TRPV5 with an IC50 of 142.6 µM. These
concentrations fall in the same range where menthol has been shown to produce cellular effects, including
toxicity in renal proximal tubular cells and changes in epithelial and mitochondrial function. This means that,
although higher than the low micromolar levels normally detected in plasma, these values are still
physiologically relevant. Therefore, the fact that menthol modulates TRPV5a at these concentrations
supports the importance of the menthol binding in TRPV5 and shows that channel modulation could occur
under conditions where menthol reaches elevated levels in specific tissues.

Response:
As the reviewer suggests, we now discuss the limitations and assumptions underlying our MD simulations
and clarify several aspects of their interpretation. We have added the following text (lines 258-271):
Although our structural data indicate a stable W583-mediated menthol-binding site, the MD trajectories
reveal additional transient interactions that show that menthol is more dynamic near the pore. Two factors
likely account for this behavior: the force field used (CGenFF) and the simulation temperature (29.8 °C).
For example, in our system the calculated dipole moment of menthol in solution is ~2.1 D, slightly higher
than the previously reported value of 1.4 D (ref). Likewise, the estimated menthol diffusivity at 4 °C is ~3.7
× 10⁻¹⁰ m²/s versus ~8 × 10⁻¹⁰ m²/s at 29.8 °C. As a result, over a 100-ns trajectory menthol would, on
average, sample ~4.7 nm at 4 °C and ~7 nm at 29.8 °C, increasing the probability of exploring alternative
poses in silico. Moreover, our simulations (~500 ns) are short relative to the timescales required for
experimental equilibration, so we cannot rule out that menthol would converge onto the single W583-
mediated pose at longer timescales or under different sampling strategies. Despite these caveats, the MD
results were essential for guiding mutagenesis, and this was validated experimentally: the I575S and
W583Q-I575S mutations drastically reduced the potency of menthol blocking, indicating that menthol
dynamically interacts with these two residues.
In addition, we expanded the Methods and Supporting Information to include all details necessary for
reproducibility, including MD protocols, force-field parameters, and relevant topology files. Specifically:
The topologies for menthol and PIO were generated using CGenFF server (https://cgenff.com,
Supplementary information), then converted from CHARMM CGenFF toppar stream files to GROMACS
format using cgenff_charmm2gmx_py3_nx2.py (https://mackerell.umaryland.edu/charmm_ff.shtml)
together with the charmm36-jul2022.ff force field (https://mackerell.umaryland.edu/charmm_ff.shtml).
Also, we now provide the complete menthol topology as well as all GROMACS commands used for energy
minimization, equilibration, production runs, and analysis.

review_generation.input:
You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

TRPV5 channels play a critical role in calcium homeostasis and are implicated in various pathophysiological
conditions. Here, we demonstrate that the monoterpene menthol, commonly used for pain and inflammation
management, is an inhibitor of TRPV5. Electrophysiology experiments reveal that menthol blocks ion
conduction through a slow blocker mechanism. Using single-particle cryo-EM, we determine the structure of
menthol-bound TRPV5, which shows menthol interacting with W583, a residue previously implicated in
channel permeation, gating and binding of endogenous modulators. These findings expand the repertoire of
TRPV5 modulators and suggest that menthol could serve as a scaffold for developing channel-targeting
modulators.

---

## Introduction

TRP channels are important regulators of cation transport in a myriad of organisms and tissues. Vanilloid
TRP channels consist of subtypes TRPV1-6 and constitute one of the most diverse subfamilies, including
members activated by temperature, lipids, and natural compounds that participate in various important
physiological and pathophysiological processes. Most TRPV channels exert their actions through calcium
(Ca2+) signaling or the regulation of Ca2+ homeostasis1.
Among the TRPV channels, TRPV5 has one of the highest permeabilities for Ca2+ ions over monovalent
cations, with a relative Ca2+ to Na+ permeability ~1002, a property it shares with its homolog protein, TRPV6,
with 70% amino acid sequence homology between both proteins 3,4. These channels are mainly found in
Ca2+-absorbing epithelia, such as kidney and intestinal tissues, where their main function is the reabsorption
of Ca2+. TRPV5 is primarily expressed in kidney epithelial cells, specifically localized to the apical
membrane of cells of the distal convoluted tubules (DCT) and connecting tubules (CNT) of the kidney,
where it functions as a highly selective epithelial calcium channel, playing a crucial role in Ca2+ reabsorption.
While TRPV5 is predominantly found in the kidney, it is also expressed at lower levels in other tissues such
as brain and bone, where it has been shown to be essential for bone resorption by osteoclasts5,6.
TRPV5 channels, similarly to most members of the TRPV subfamily, form a functional tetramer at the cell
surface assembled by subunits containing six transmembrane domains with large intracellular N- and C-
termini. The pore domain consists of the S5, loop, and S6 segments of each subunit, which assemble
symmetrically in a four-fold structure to create a central ion conduction pathway7,8. The re-entrant pore loop
of each subunit forms the extracellular part of the pore and functions as a selectivity filter, determining ion
permeability, with a single aspartic residue at position 542 acting as a Ca2+ selectivity filter9,10. The S6
helices line the intracellular pore and form the gate at its narrowest part. TRPV5 inactivates in response to
Ca2+ entry, a process mediated by calmodulin (CaM) binding to the channel11 promoted by the interaction
between the last residue at the end of the S6 gate of the channel, the highly conserved W583, with a C-
terminal lysine of the CaM, which blocks the flow of ions through the pore7,12. The disruption of CaM binding
leads to increased TRPV5 expression at the plasma membrane by avoiding channel retention in the
endoplasmic reticulum13. The tryptophan residue W583 is highly conserved in TRPV5 across various
species, but it is absent in other members of the TRPV family and is crucial for channel gating14.
TRPV5 channels display marked inward rectification and are constitutively open at negative potentials,
allowing for passive entry of cations into cells at the resting membrane potential. Regulation of TRPV5 is
mainly carried out by the control of phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PI(4,5)P2) lipid concentration,
which binds between the N-linker, S4-S5 linker , and the S6 helix to keep the channel open12. Signaling by
vitamin D, which mostly regulates expression of protein at the plasma membrane15 and by parathyroid
hormone, which acts through PKA phosphorylation16, also regulate the channel. The long-chain lipid acyl-
coenzyme A (LC-CoA) is a highly efficient activator of TRPV5 that binds to the same site as the endogenous
ligand PI(4,5)P2 and induces very similar conformation changes to open the channel17.
TRPV5 channels have a relatively limited pharmacology, with only a few known additional endogenous
activators, such as PKC activator 1-oleoyl-acetyl-sn-glycerol (OAG) and the b-glucuronidase, Klotho, that
hydrolyzes extracellular sugar residues of TRPV518,19. Conversely, TRPV5 is inhibited by synthetic
compounds, including TH-117720, cannabinoids21, and a higher specificity inhibitor, ZINC1798899022.
Econazole and miconazole are antifungal agents that act as inhibitors of TRPV5. These compounds bind to
a specific pocket situated between the S4 and S5 transmembrane domains23, which is shared with TRPV6
channels24 and likely act as allosteric inhibitors of channel opening. Additionally, ruthenium red is a non-
selective inhibitor of many ion channels. In the case of TRPV5, it binds to the pore domain, likely blocking
conduction and stabilizing the channel in a closed state24,25.
Menthol is a highly-membrane permeable monoterpene alcohol derived from the mint plant (Mentha sp.)
and a known activator of cold-sensing TRPM8 channels26. Menthol is an interesting compound that has
been associated with renal toxicity and impaired intestinal mobility27,28, which could be mediated in part by
TRPV5 and TRPV6 ion channels. Menthol also activates or inhibits other TRP channels, such as TRPV3,
TRPV1 and TRPA1, although the structural mechanisms involved are not known29–32. TRPV5 and TRPV6
are only 30 % similar to other TRPVs which suggests that different mechanisms of modulation by menthol.
Given its potential effects on renal and gut physiology, and lack of mechanistic information, we explored
menthol’s actions on TRPV5 channels. Here we show that it acts as a blocker of TRPV5. We show that
menthol inhibits current through TRPV5 expressed in HEK293 cells by producing long-lived closures, likely
corresponding to slow blocking events. We solve the structure of rabbit TRPV5 in complex with menthol by
cryo-EM and find that a key determinant of menthol inhibition is a tryptophane residue at position 583
located at the intracellular entrance of the pore. Mutations W583Q and I575S readily reduce the effects of
menthol, suggesting that they are important mediators of the menthol interaction. Our results expand the
repertoire of inhibitors of TRPV5 channels and have implications to understand possible effects of menthol
in renal physiology.

---

## Results

Menthol inhibits TRPV5 via a slow blocker mechanism.
First, we assessed the effect of menthol on the rabbit TRPV5 (rbTRPV5) by applying 500 μM menthol to the
external face of the membrane in outside-out patch configuration. Menthol rapidly inhibited more than 50%
of the current at all voltages without altering current kinetics (Figure 1a). This inhibitory effect was largely
reversible and occurred in a dose-dependent manner across all tested voltages (Figure 1b, c, d). Fitting the
dose-response curve with a Hill equation (Equation (1)), we determined a half-maximal inhibitory
concentration (IC ) of 142.6 μM and a Hill coefficient (n ) of 0.75, suggesting that a single menthol
50 H
molecule is sufficient to induce inhibition (Figure 1e).
Interestingly, menthol block of TRPV5 is slightly voltage dependent, with the blocked fraction reduced at
less negative potentials (Figure 1f). Because menthol does not carry a net charge, we sought to explain this
voltage-dependence by exploring the predictions of a multiple state model for block. We adapted a
previously published three state gating model of TRPV5 14 and incorporated open state block (Scheme I,
Figure 1g). To constrain the model, we measured the voltage-dependence of single-channel channel
openings, which indeed show that TRPV5 gating is intrinsically voltage dependent (Supplementary figure 1a
and c). Scheme I explains the voltage dependence of menthol block because it is coupled to the open state
and opening is itself voltage-dependent (Figure 1g). This model also accounts for both the voltage and
dose-dependence of block with the same set of parameters (Figure 1e).
Since the sequence of the inner pore region is highly conserved between mammalian TRPV5 and 6
channels, we examined the effect of menthol on the human TRPV5 orthologue and the related human
TRPV6 channel, finding that both channels were also blocked by menthol with similar efficacy
(Supplementary figure 2).
To further investigate the mechanism by which menthol inhibits TRPV5 currents, we analyzed single-
channel recordings. Recordings from patches containing a single TRPV5 channel at -100 mV showed that
gating was characterized by openings that occur in bursts (Figure 2a). The single-channel current amplitude
remained unaffected by menthol, as indicated by all-points amplitude histograms of selected current
segments (Figure 2b). In contrast, menthol increased both the frequency and duration of non-conducting
events in a dose-dependent manner. To quantify this effect, we idealized channel openings and compiled
open and closed dwell time histograms (Figure 2c and d). The gating behavior of TRPV5 shows three
exponential components in the closed-time distribution and two components in the open-time distribution
(Table 1 and 2). The number of exponential components in these distributions represents the minimum
number of closed or open states. In this case, data indicates there are three closed or non-conductive states
and one or two open states. These kinetics are consistent with the model in Scheme I (Figure 1g), although
this is not a definitive model.
Further analysis of single-channel recordings shows that menthol induces a concentration-dependent
lengthening of the longer closed-state durations, while reducing the slow component of the open-state
durations, consistent with menthol blocking ion conduction and shortening the length of bursts of openings
(Figure 2e, f and Table 1 and 2). These findings indicate that menthol inhibition occurs via a blocking
mechanism that does not alter single-channel current amplitude, a characteristic feature of slow channel
blockers33.
Structural mechanism of TRPV5 blockade by menthol.
To gain structural insight into the molecular mechanism by which menthol blocks TRPV5, we determined the
cryoEM structure of full-length rabbit TRPV5 in complex with menthol. A priori, it is unclear whether menthol
solely blocks the channel or also induces an alternative conformational state to close the channel. Given
that TRPV5 adopts an open state in the presence of PI(4,5)P , we initiated our experiments with a PIP₂-
2
activated channel and subsequently applied menthol to assess its effect, which are similar conditions to
those in which current recordings are performed. First, purified TRPV5 embedded in lipid nanodiscs was
incubated with 400 μM PI(4,5)P for 45 min to activate the channel, followed by the addition of 1 mM
2
menthol and further incubation for 30 min before vitrification. CryoEM data processing yielded a structure at
3.37 Å resolution in a single conformational state, without imposed symmetry, which we refer to as
TRPV5 , (Supplementary figure 3 and Supplementary table 3).
PIP2+Menthol
The TRPV5 structure reveals a clear density at the intracellular entrance of the pore, positioned
PIP2+Menthol
between the S6 helices, consistent with presence of the menthol molecule (Figure 3a, b). Importantly, this
density was not observed in the previous published TRPV5 structures24,25 (Supplementary figure 4d).
PIP2
The model suggests that one molecule of menthol is primarily coordinated by two W583 residues, forming a
potential hydrogen bond (2.8 Å) between its hydroxyl group and the amide group of W583, as well as a CH-
π interaction (3.3 Å) with the indole ring of the adjacent W583 residue. Notably, W583 has been previously
shown to coordinate the binding of a lysine residue from CaM, which also inhibits TRPV57,34, and to stabilize
the ligand ciss-22a in TRPV635.
Comparing TRPV5 structure with the control structure, TRPV5 in the presence of PI(4,5)P
PIP2+Menthol 2
(TRPV5 )17, we found that the pore remains in a semi-open state (RMSD=0.5 Å) (Figure 3c-i). Specially,
PIP2
the presence of menthol within the pore slightly reduces the pore diameter at I575. This effect is
accompanied by a conformational change in the rotameric angle of W583, which shifts to accommodate
hydrophobic interactions with the ligand. As a result, the pore at W583 adopts a conformation closely
resembling the apo state (Figure 3f). Consistent with this observation, we detected densities at the PI(4,5)P
2
binding site that resemble partially a PI(4,5)P molecule (Supplementary figure 4e). These densities, as
2
previously reported, are in contact with the basic residues R302, R305, K484, and R584, where the
interaction with R584 being one of the most important for inducing the open conformational state12,17,34. Both
our patch-clamp and cryo-EM results suggest that menthol blocks TRPV5 in the open state, a mechanism
like that of CaM, further reinforcing the role of W583 as a key regulatory site for channel modulation.
Menthol binds to W583 in TRPV5 channels.
To functionally validate this interaction, we introduced the W583Q mutation, which removes potential
hydrophobic and aromatic interactions while preserving side-chain size and introducing a polar group. The
W583Q mutation significantly reduced menthol-induced inhibition, shifting the dose-response curve to
higher concentrations (IC = 3.7 mM, Figure 4a and c), indicating that W583 is critical for menthol binding,
50
as suggested by the cryo-EM structure. Single-channel recording confirmed the reduced inhibition by
menthol of this mutant. W583Q channels exhibited distinct gating behavior comparted to WT. Whereas WT
TRPV5 opens in bursts, W583Q channels displayed continuous opening and closing events (Supplementary
Figure 5), similar to the previously reported W583L mutation14. The closed-time distribution contained two
time-constants that remined unaffected by menthol, while the open-time distribution was fitted with two
exponentials components (Supplementary table 1 and 2), consistent with Scheme I, indicating that the
mutations did not greatly alter channel gating. W583Q showed a slight reduction in the slow component with
increasing menthol concentrations. At the highest concentrations, in contrast to WT channels, menthol
reduced the single-channel current amplitude in W583Q, suggesting that in the absence of a tryptophane at
position 583, menthol behaves as a fast blocker, accounting for the remaining block (Supplementary Figure
5d).
Despite this mutation producing a gain-of-function phenotype, shifting channel open probability and the I-V
curve to more positive potentials (Supplementary figure 1 and Supplementary figure 6, respectively),
W583Q retained the inward rectification characteristic of TRPV5 (Figure 4a and Supplementary Figure 6a).
Furthermore, the mutant was also blocked by the pore blocker ruthenium red (RR) with an IC close to that
50
of WT channels, indicating that the mutation does not alter the pore architecture and that its effect is specific
to block by menthol (Supplementary figure 7).
Menthol block was also tested in the previously characterized W583A mutant, for which a cryo EM structure
exists7 (Figure 4b). Similarly to W583Q, W583A showed reduced menthol block (Figure 4b and c). The
observation that both small or large polar substitutions at position W583 greatly impair menthol binding,
supports the importance of hydrophobic interactions in stabilizing menthol binding.
Our cryo-EM structure further suggests that menthol may be stabilized at its binding site through a hydrogen
bond between its hydroxyl group and the indole of W583 (Figure 4d). To test this interaction, we substituted
W583 by a phenylalanine, which lacks an indole group and cannot form hydrogen bonds. The W583F
mutant exhibited a right-shifted menthol dose-response curve, suggesting reduced affinity (Figure 4e, f).
Similarly, W583Y, which retains hydrophobicity but introduces a hydroxyl group, also impaired menthol
block. These results highlight the requirement for specific indole chemistry of tryptophane at position W583
for menthol coordination (Figure 4e, f).
Since many W583 mutation produce gain of function phenotypes (14 and Supplementary figure 6), as control
we introduced mutations at nearby positions. Mutations M578L and G579A, which are localized in the inner
gate and near W583, yielded inwardly rectifying channels with menthol sensitivity similar to WT, confirming
that the effects W583 substitutions on menthol block are specific and not due to gross alteration of pore
structure (Supplementary figure 8). Importantly, G579A has previously been reported to yield stable
macroscopic currents under divalent-free recording conditions14. In the same study, M578 was not identified
as a major contributor to pore constriction, consistent with our observation that the M578L mutation does not
affect menthol sensitivity (Supplementary figure 8).
As presented in the previous section, our structural and functional data reveal that menthol binds to the
intracellular entrance of the TRPV5 pore, specifically interacting with residue W583 while the pore remains
open. To probe the dynamics of menthol pore occupancy, we ran 500 ns all-atom molecular dynamics (MD)
simulations of the open-state TRPV5
PIP2
structure (PDB: 8FFO), with menthol molecules initially placed
randomly in the aqueous phase. Our results showed that the protein stabilized after ~20 ns (RMSD = 2-4 Å,
Supplementary figure 9e), with minor fluctuations (RMSF ~2 Å) observed at the intracellular entrance of the
pore (Supplementary figure 9f), suggesting that the presence of menthol does not induce substantial
conformational changes in the protein. All four simulations replicas showed menthol entering and occupying
the pore from intracellular site (Supplementary figure 9a and b). Trajectory analysis revealed that menthol
molecules can permeate the plasma membrane (Supplementary figure 9d). No Na+ permeation events
occurred during any menthol-occupied state. To quantify the position of menthol relative to the pore, we
measured its distance from I575 (Supplementary figure 9a, b). Unexpectedly, menthol remained at W583 for
only a brief period, forming transient hydrogen bonds lasting 0.1-0.5 ns, before establishing an interaction
with other residues inside the pore, particularly I575, which appeared to stabilize menthol. Once a menthol
occupied the pore, additional menthol molecules interacted more frequently with W583 (Supplementary
figure 9c), suggesting that both W583 and I575 are key residues involved in menthol-mediated TRPV5
blockade.
Effect of mutations at position I575.
To investigate the role of I575 in menthol binding, as suggested by the MD simulations, we tested the I575S
mutant, which should eliminate hydrophobic interactions and introduce a polar residue. This mutation also
diminished menthol inhibition, shifting the dose-response curve to higher concentrations and decreasing the
fraction of blocked current, even at high menthol concentrations (Figure 5a, d, e). The magnitude of this
effect was comparable to that observed in W583Q, suggesting that menthol interacts with I575, or
alternatively, that the presence of a polar residue at position 575 disrupts menthol interactions with W583.
As a control, we tested the I575L mutation, which preserves a hydrophobic residue but could alter sidechain
packing near the protein backbone and should induce little deformation. This mutant retains the menthol
blocking affinity of WT (Figure 5b, d, e). The results indicate that menthol might move from its W583 binding
site to a deeper position within the pore and requires a hydrophobic amino acid at position 575.
Finally, we examined the W583Q-I575S double mutant. These channels remained inwardly rectifying and
retained their affinity for the pore blocker ruthenium red (Supplementary figure 7), indicating that the
combined mutations did not drastically alter TRPV5 gating. However, the double mutant exhibited
significantly reduced susceptibility to menthol inhibition (Figure 5c, d, e), almost completely eliminating block
by menthol, confirming that both W583 and I575 are essential for menthol binding and TRPV5 blockade.

---

## Methods

Molecular biology and cell transfection
The gene encoding full-length rabbit TRPV5 (rbTRPV5; UNIPROT id: Q9XSM3·TRPV5_RABIT) ion channel
cloned in pCINeo/IRES-GFP was a gift from Dr. Tibor Rohacs (Rutgers University). This is a bicistronic
plasmid containing both the channel and a GFP (UNIPROT id: Q17105_AEQVI) sequence under separate
promotors, allowing identification of transfected cells by looking for GFP-fluorescent cells. Human TRPV5
(UNIPROT id: Q9NQA5·TRPV5_HUMAN) was subcloned in the pCDNA3.1(+) vector and was a gift from Dr.
Sharona Gordon (University of Washington). TRPV6 (UNIPROT id: Q9H1D0·_HUMAN) was cloned from
human placenta and was donated to us by Dr. Tibor Rohacs54. Residue numbers refer to the human TRPV5
sequence (729 amino acids); the corresponding regions in human TRPV6 (725 aa) and rabbit TRPV5 (730
aa) are conserved, so numbering is the same across all three proteins in this study.
Single and double mutations were introduced into the rbTRPV5 gene using mutagenic oligonucleotides in
whole-plasmid PCR reactions employing KOD Hot Start DNA polymerase (Novagen-Millipore Corp.)
according to the manufacturer's instructions. PCR products were treated with 1 μl DpnI restriction enzyme
(New England Biolabs) and incubated 5 hrs at 37 °C to remove the parent plasmid. The samples were
transformed into DH5α E. coli competent cells. For each mutant, five colonies were picked and inoculated in

confirmed by automatic sequencing.

serum and 1 % of antibiotics (penicillin and streptomycin) (Invitrogen USA), at 37°C, in a 5 % CO

(Trypsin-EDTA) in 35mm culture dishes over glass coverslips for subsequent electrophysiology assays.
Experiments were performed 19–24 hours after transfection with 1 μg of rbTRPV5-IRES-GFP (wild-type or
mutant). Due to the low cell viability observed after expression of most mutants, a separate plasmid
encoding pEGFP-N1 was introduced to enhance the identification of transfected cells. For single-channel
recordings, 25 ng of wild-type or mutant DNA for 24 hours was used, along with 100 ng of the pEGFP-N1
plasmid, to identify transfected cells.

Preparation of menthol and ruthenium red solutions
(-)-Menthol was obtained from Santa Cruz Biotechnology, dissolved in absolute ethanol to form a stock
solution at 200 mM, and then diluted from this stock in recording solution at the desired concentration (1 M,
10 M, 100 M, 500 M, 1 mM, 3 mM). These working solutions were then sonicated for 5-10 minutes
before use and prepared fresh for every recording day. The higher concentration of (-)-menthol used (3 mM)
had a final ethanol concentration of 1.5 %, thus, 1.5 % ethanol in recording solution was used as a control in

Ruthenium red (Ammoniated Ruthenium Oxychloride, Sigma-Aldrich) was prepared as a stock solution at
100 M in water. Dilutions where prepared from this stock to reach concentrations of 0.5 nM, 1 nM, 10 nM,
100 nM, 500 nM, 1 M.
Igor Pro 8 software (Wavemetrics) was used for analysis, including fitting, single-channel analyses,
statistical analysis and figure preparation. Data were assumed to follow a normal distribution, and
hypothesis testing was performed using unpaired, two-tailed Student’s t-tests.
TRPV5 protein preparation
TRPV5 preparation and purification followed the protocol described in34. Briefly, the rabbit TRPV5 with a C-
terminal 1D4 epitope tag in a YepM vector 23 was transfected into BJ5457 Saccharomyces cerevisiae
(ATCC) using an alkali-cation yeast transformation kit (MP Biomedicals), according to the instructions of the
manufacturer. Transformed cells were plated on SD-Leu agar plates and allowed to grow at 30°C for 2
days. 30-50 colonies were picked from a plate and inoculated into a single 125 mL starter culture containing
SD-Leu media and 10% v/v glycerol. The culture was incubated at 30°C until reaching the top of the log
phase (OD 1.0–1.4). After confirmation of protein expression by Western blot, the cells were grown at 30°C
with shaking at 200 rpm in 2.5 L of media per flask until OD of 1.0–1.4 was reached. Cells were harvested
by centrifugation at 3000 × g, resuspended in storage buffer (25 mM Tris-HCl, pH 8.0, 300 mM sucrose, and
1 mM PMSF) on ice, and then spun down at 3000 × g to discard the supernatant. Cell pellets were
subsequently stored at −80°C. This expression culture was propagated using 15 mL of the previous growth
at OD 1.0–1.4 for several days until the desired amount was obtained.
Approximately 60 L of growth cells were thawed and resuspended in 300 mL of homogenization buffer (25
mM Tris-HCl, pH 8.0, 300 mM sucrose, 5 mM EDTA, and protease inhibitor cocktail). The resuspended cells
were lysed using a M110Y microfluidizer (Microfluidics) at 100-120 psi. The membranes were separated
from cellular debris by centrifugation at 3,000 × g for 10 min, followed by centrifugation of the supernatant at
14,000 × g for 35 min. The membranes obtained from the previous spin were then pelleted at 100,000 × g
for 1 h. The pelleted membranes were harvested and resuspended on ice using a 15 mL tissue
homogenizer (Kontes Duall with PTFE pestle) in buffer containing 25 mM Tris-HCl, pH 8.0, 300 mM
sucrose, and 1 mM PMSF, and stored at −80°C.
TRPV5 was solubilized from the thawed membranes in solubilization buffer (20 mM HEPES, pH 8.0, 150
mM NaCl, 2 mM TCEP, and 0.87 mM LMNG). The insoluble fraction was separated by centrifugation at
100,000 × g for 1 h. The resulting supernatant was incubated with 1D4-antibody coupled to CnBr-activated
Sepharose beads for 3 h. The beads were collected on a gravity flow column, washed with wash buffer (20
mM HEPES, pH 8.0, 150 mM NaCl, 2 mM TCEP, and 0.064 mM DMNG). The beads were incubated with
elution buffer (20 mM HEPES, pH 8.0, 150 mM NaCl, 2 mM TCEP, and 0.064 mM DMNG, 3 mg/mL 1D4
peptide) overnight. TRPV5 was eluted in 1 mL fractions every 5 minutes. Peak fractions were pooled and
concentrated using a 100-kDa concentrator (Millipore). For reconstitution into nanodiscs, an equimolar
amount of MSP2N2 protein was incubated with the detergent-solubilized TRPV5 in the presence of soy
polar lipids and DMNG detergent in a 1 mL reaction volume. The molar ratio of TRPV5:MSP2N2:lipid:DMNG
in mixture was 1:1:200:500. Lipids and DMNG were dissolved in 20 mM HEPES, pH 8.0, 150 mM NaCl, 2
mM TCEP (SEC buffer). The reaction mixture was incubated on ice for 30 min, followed by the addition of
~30 μL of Bio-Beads. The mixture was rotated at 4°C for 1 h. The supernatant was transferred to a new
tube, and another 30 μL of fresh Bio-Beads was added before rotating at 4°C overnight to complete the
reaction. Reconstituted TRPV5 was subjected to a Superose 6 increase 10/300 GL column (GE Healthcare)
equilibrated with SEC buffer. Fractions containing nanodisc reconstituted TRPV5 were pooled and
concentrated to 2.57 mg/ml.
Cryo-EM sample preparation and data collection
TRPV5 sample was incubated with 400 μM diC8-PI(4,5)P (Echelon Biosciences, Cat# P-4508) for
PIP2+Menthol 2
45 minutes and 1 mM Menthol (Sigma-Aldrich, Cat# 2216-51-5) for 30 minutes, corresponding to a 1:53:132
(TRPV5:PIP2:Menthol) molar ratio. Menthol was solubilized in 100% ethanol (200 mM) and then diluted at
15% in SEC buffer (30 mM). Final sample contained 1% ethanol. 3 μL TRPV5 sample was applied
PIP2+Menthol
to glow-discharged 1.2/1.3 Quantifoil Holey Carbon Grids (Quantifoil Micro Tools) using a Vitrobot Mark IV
(Thermo Scientific). The sample was blotted in a chamber at 4°C and 100% humidity for 6 s at 0 blotting
force before being freezing in liquid ethane.
Samples were imaged on a Titan Krios G3i 300 kV electron microscope with a Gatan K3 direct electron
detector. 40-42 frame movies were collected with a nominal dose of 41-43 e−/Å2. Super-resolution images
for all datasets were collected at 105,000 magnification with a pixel size of 0.415 Å/pixel.
Data processing
Two datasets of 5,427 (DSA) and 4,736 (DSB) movies were collected and processed in cryoSPARC
v4.4.158,59. Movies were patch motion corrected with a Fourier-crop factor of 0.5 and an alignment resolution
of 3 Å, followed by the patch CTF estimation. Micrographs were manually curated based on a maximum
CTF fit resolution of 8 Å. The template for autopicking were created with 94,896 (DSA) and 94,858 (DSB)
particles blob picked from subsets of 300 micrographs from each dataset and used for extraction. 1,281,269
and 1,491,899 particles were extracted and binned by a factor of 4 with a box size of 72 pixels from DSA
and DSB, respectively. These particles were 2D classified with 100 classes, resulting in 360,885 (DSA) and
225,211 (DSB) good particles that were re-extracted. A three-class heterogeneous refinement was
performed to separate good particles with the TRPV5 apo map (EMD-25716
[https://www.ebi.ac.uk/emdb/EMD-25716]) as a reference, resulting in a good class of 233,564 (DSA)
and 160,664 (DSB) particles at 0.83 and 1.66 Å/pix, respectively. Particles were refined with a non-uniform
refinement with no symmetry to generate the initial model12. Particles from DSA were subjected to 3D
classification with 5 classes focusing on the pore region. The best class, totaling 57,516 particles, were
combined to produce a map with a resolution of 3.53 Å with no symmetry at 0.83 Å/pix. These particles were
subjected to two rounds of heterogeneous refinement and non-uniform refinement, resulting in 33,086
particles, which produced a structure with a resolution of 3.44 Å. Similarly, 22,633 particles were obtained
from DSB after subjected to two rounds of heterogeneous refinement and non-uniform refinement: these
particles generated a structure with a resolution of 3.83 Å. Both datasets were combined and
heterogeneously refined into three volumes. The best structure form with 42.348 particles was refined with a
non-uniform refinement to produce the final map with a resolution of 3.37 Å with no symmetry.
The local resolution was determined in cryoSPARC, and the angular distributions were generated with the
UCSF pyem package.
Model building
The TRPV5 model (8FFO [https://doi.org/10.2210/pdb8FFO/pdb]) (Lee et al. 2023) was used as the
PIP2
initial model and manually adjusted in ISOLDE60. Lipids, PI(4,5)P (PIO), and Menthol (IT9), obtained from
2
the ePDB database, were docked and manually adjusted in COOT61. Real Space_Refinement and eLBOW
from the PHENIX software62 were used to refine and to generate ligand restraints, respectively.
Pore profiles were determined using HOLE63. Chimera, ChimeraX, and PyMol were used for analysis,
visualization and figure generation.
Molecular dynamics simulations
The TRPV5 coordinate model (PDB ID: 8FFO [https://doi.org/10.2210/pdb8FFO/pdb]) (Lee et al. 2023),
PIP₂
oriented using the 6DMU structure from the Positioning of Proteins in Membranes (OPM) server
(http://opm.phar.umich.edu/server.php), was embedded in a 1-palmitoyl-2-oleoyl-sn-glycerol-3-
phosphocholine (POPC) lipid bilayer (606 molecules) along with phosphatidylinositol-4,5-bisphosphate
(model with PIO, 4 molecules) and ergosterol (8 molecules) at pH 7.3. The protein-membrane complex was
solvated with TIP3 water, 100 mM NaCl, and approximately 8 mM menthol, resulting in a system containing
84,087 water molecules, 203 Na⁺, 151 Cl⁻, and 20 menthol molecules within a 160 × 160 × 160 Å³
simulation box (Supplementary Table 4). The membrane-protein system was built using the CHARMM-GUI
membrane builder65 (http://www.charmm-gui.org). The topologies for menthol and PIO were generated
using CGenFF server (https://cgenff.com, Supplementary information), then converted from CHARMM
CGenFF toppar stream files to GROMACS format using cgenff_charmm2gmx_py3_nx2.py
(https://mackerell.umaryland.edu/charmm_ff.shtml) together with the charmm36-jul2022.ff force field
(https://mackerell.umaryland.edu/charmm_ff.shtml). Menthol molecules were placed randomly in the
aqueous region.
Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations were performed using the GPU-accelerated GROMACS 2024.366
package with the CHARMM36m force field67. The system was energy-minimized and equilibrated using the
steepest descent algorithm in CHARMM-GUI without modifications in configuration files (Supplementary
information). In the final equilibration step, the system remained stable with a total energy of −2.75 × 10⁶ ±
691.63 kJ/mol, where the potential energy was −3.76 × 10⁶ ± 1340.85 kJ/mol and the kinetic energy was
1.01 × 10⁶ ± 1171.37 kJ/mol. The temperature remained at 303.18 ± 0.35 K, and the volume at 3631.97 ±
1.17 nm³. The protein RMSD remained at 0.058 ± 0.008 nm. The temperature was maintained at 303 K
using a Nosé−Hoover thermostat, and the pressure at 1 bar using a Parrinello−Rahman barostat. Bond
constraints were applied using the LINCS algorithm. Long-range electrostatic interactions were calculated
using the Particle Mesh Ewald (PME) method with a 12 Å cutoff and updated every 2 fs. Van der Waals
interactions were switched at 10 Å with a 12 Å cutoff. Production simulations consisted of four independent
500 ns runs at 0 mV membrane voltage, and trajectory analyses were performed using GROMACS tools
and VMD.
Molecular docking
Docking of menthol into the cryoEM structure was carried out with AutoDock Vina implemented in
SwisDock68. We used a box of 18 x 18 x 8 Å comprising the position of W583. Default parameters were
used with an exhaustivity of 64.
Data availability
All cryo-EM data generated in these studies are available upon request from Vera Y. Moiseenkova-Bell
(vmb@pennmedicine.upenn.edu). The cryo-EM maps have been deposited in the Electron Microscopy Data
Bank (EMDB) under accession code EMD-70173 [https://www.ebi.ac.uk/pdbe/entry/emdb/EMD-70173]
(TRPV5 ); EMD-25716 [https://www.ebi.ac.uk/em db/EMD-25716] (TRPV5 ); EMD-29049
PIP2+Menthol Apo
[https://www.ebi.ac.uk/emdb/EMD-29049] (TRPV5 ). The atomic coordinates have been deposited in the
PIP2
Protein Data Bank (PDB) under accession code 9O6G [https://doi.org/10.2210/pdb9O6G/pdb]
(TRPV5 ); 8TF2 [https://doi.org/10.2210/pdb8TF2/pdb] (TRPV5 ): 8FFO
PIP2+Menthol Apo
[https://doi.org/10.2210/pdb8FFO/pdb] (TRPV5 ). All molecular dynamics trajectories can be accessed on
PIP2
Zenodo [https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.18472580]69. All other data is included in the paper. Source data are
provided with this paper.
